christianity_2_kings_20_17.context: God declares that all valuable possessions in Hezekiah's palace will be taken to Babylon, leaving nothing behind. God also says that Hezekiah's sons will be taken as eunuchs to Babylon.

christianity_2_kings_20_18.meaning: Enduring hardships for the sake of faith and trust in God's plan.
christianity_2_kings_20_18.context: God reveals that Hezekiah's sons will be taken as eunuchs to Babylon as a consequence of the Babylonian invasion.

christianity_2_kings_20_7.meaning: Trust in God and have faith. When facing challenges or illness, seek divine guidance and follow it. In this case, Hezekiah asked for a sign, but faith involves trusting in God's plan without needing tangible proof.
christianity_2_kings_20_7.context: This verse is from the Bible, specifically in the book of 2 Kings. It tells the story of King Hezekiah of Judah who becomes sick and asks the prophet Isaiah for a sign from God to show He will heal him. Isaiah suggests taking a fig cake and placing it on a boil on Hezekiah's body to see if it heals him.

christianity_2_kings_20_8.meaning: Ask for wisdom and guidance from spiritual leaders. When uncertain about a situation, consult with those who have knowledge and understanding to receive insight.
christianity_2_kings_20_8.context: King Hezekiah asks Isaiah the prophet for a sign from God about his healing. Hezekiah wants to know if God will heal him before he dies.

christianity_2_kings_20_9.meaning: Faith in God's promises and trust in His plan. When faced with a challenge or uncertain situation, have faith in God's ability to provide a solution or outcome.
christianity_2_kings_20_9.context: This verse continues the story from 2 Kings 20. Isaiah tells Hezekiah that God will add ten years to his life if he agrees to let the sun's shadow go backward ten steps. Hezekiah accepts the sign.

christianity_2_kings_20_10.meaning: Gratitude for God's blessings and recognizing His power. When experiencing blessings or answered prayers, express gratitude and reflect on God's greatness.
christianity_2_kings_20_10.context: King Hezekiah follows Isaiah's sign and the sun's shadow goes back ten steps. Hezekiah realizes God's power and gratitude.

christianity_2_kings_20_11.meaning: God can change time and nature to show his power and keep his promises to his people.
christianity_2_kings_20_11.context: King Hezekiah asked God for a sign to prove he would live after being very sick.

christianity_2_kings_20_12.meaning: News of God's miracles travels fast, drawing attention from powerful foreign rulers and nations.
christianity_2_kings_20_12.context: A king from Babylon sent gifts and letters to Hezekiah after hearing he was sick.

christianity_2_kings_20_13.meaning: Showing off wealth to strangers can be dangerous and may lead to losing what you have.
christianity_2_kings_20_13.context: Hezekiah proudly showed the Babylonian visitors all his gold, silver, and weapons in his palace.

christianity_2_kings_20_14.meaning: We should be careful about who we trust and what we share with outsiders.
christianity_2_kings_20_14.context: The prophet Isaiah asked Hezekiah where the visitors came from and what they said to him.

christianity_2_kings_21_3.meaning: He followed bad examples, ignoring God’s rules, and led people into wrong worship.
christianity_2_kings_21_3.context: He rebuilt forbidden temples, made altars for Baal, and worshiped sky gods, like Ahab did.

christianity_2_kings_21_4.meaning: He pretended to honor God, but actually tried to control God’s presence for his own power.
christianity_2_kings_21_4.context: He put altars in God’s house, claiming God would name Himself in Jerusalem.

christianity_2_kings_21_5.meaning: He mixed false worship with true worship, confusing people and disrespecting God’s holy place.
christianity_2_kings_21_5.context: He built altars for sky gods inside the main courts of God’s temple.

christianity_2_kings_21_6.meaning: He used dangerous practices to test God, showing disrespect and causing trouble for everyone.
christianity_2_kings_21_6.context: He forced his son through fire, used magic, and dealt with spirits, doing evil to anger God.

christianity_2_kings_21_7.meaning: Putting false gods in holy places shows deep disrespect. We must keep our worship pure and focused only on the true God.
christianity_2_kings_21_7.context: King Manasseh placed a pagan idol inside the sacred temple that God had chosen for His name to dwell forever.

christianity_2_kings_21_8.meaning: Obedience to divine rules brings stability and protection. Following God's guidance ensures we stay secure and blessed in our lives.
christianity_2_kings_21_8.context: God promised to keep Israel safe in their land if they obeyed all the laws given through Moses.

christianity_2_kings_21_9.meaning: Following bad leaders leads to worse sin. We must reject evil influences and choose to do what is right.
christianity_2_kings_21_9.context: The people ignored God and followed King Manasseh into evil ways that were worse than the nations God had already destroyed.

christianity_2_kings_21_10.meaning: God speaks through messengers to correct us. We should listen to wise guidance that helps us return to the right path.
christianity_2_kings_21_10.context: God used his prophets to speak his message to the people, warning them about their disobedience and calling them back.

christianity_2_kings_20_20.meaning: Good leaders prepare for hard times by working hard to keep their people safe and secure.
christianity_2_kings_20_20.context: Hezekiah built water systems to protect Jerusalem from enemy armies during difficult times of war.

christianity_2_kings_20_21.meaning: Life changes when leaders pass away and new rulers must step up to guide the people.
christianity_2_kings_20_21.context: King Hezekiah died and was buried with his ancestors while his son Manasseh took the throne.

christianity_2_kings_21_1.meaning: Young leaders can hold power for a long time and shape the future of their nation.
christianity_2_kings_21_1.context: Manasseh became king at age twelve and ruled Jerusalem for fifty five years with his mother.

christianity_2_kings_21_2.meaning: Following bad examples leads people away from truth and causes harm to their spiritual lives.
christianity_2_kings_21_2.context: Manasseh did evil things that God hated by copying the bad habits of other pagan nations.

christianity_2_kings_21_19.meaning: Amon became a king at a young age and ruled for two years. His mother's background is mentioned, but the focus is on his short reign and the lack of information about his reign's content.
christianity_2_kings_21_19.context: This verse talks about Amon, a king who started ruling at the age of 22. He ruled for two years in Jerusalem and his mother's name was Meshullemeth from Jotbah.

christianity_2_kings_21_20.meaning: Amon, like his father Manasseh, committed sins and displeased God.
christianity_2_kings_21_20.context: Amon followed the evil ways of his father Manasseh, doing what was displeasing to God.

christianity_2_kings_21_21.meaning: Amon continued his father's idol worship and followed his father's religious path.
christianity_2_kings_21_21.context: Amon continued the idol worship started by his father and followed his father's path.

christianity_2_kings_21_22.meaning: Amon left the true God and chose to follow other gods, just like his father.
christianity_2_kings_21_22.context: Amon abandoned God, the true God of his ancestors, and chose to follow other gods instead.

christianity_2_kings_21_15.meaning: Us that consistently doing evil deeds can lead to anger and disappointment from higher powers, just like King Manasseh's actions angered God. It emphasizes the importance of following righteousness and avoiding past mistakes made by our ancestors.
christianity_2_kings_21_15.context: This verse is from the Christian Bible, specifically in 2 Kings 21:15. It talks about King Manasseh of Judah who committed great sins, including angering God by continuing evil actions since the time of his fathers coming out of Egypt.

christianity_2_kings_21_16.meaning: The consequences of committing atrocities and turning away from the true faith. Manasseh's actions led to great suffering among the people and his own downfall as a king.
christianity_2_kings_21_16.context: In Christianity, 2 Kings 21:16 mentions King Manasseh who caused much innocent bloodshed in Jerusalem and added to his sins by worshipping false gods. This verse describes his evil deeds.

christianity_2_kings_21_17.meaning: This verse shows the importance of recording history and learning from the mistakes of past leaders like King Manasseh. It teaches us the significance of documenting our experiences and reflecting on them to grow as individuals and societies.
christianity_2_kings_21_17.context: 2 Kings 21:17 in the Christian Bible states that after Manasseh's death, the Chronicles of the kings of Judah document his entire life, including his sins.

christianity_2_kings_21_18.meaning: This verse demonstrates the cycle of kingship and the influence of family lineage. Amon's reign followed his father's actions, emphasizing the importance of choosing righteous leaders and the consequences of evil lineage.
christianity_2_kings_21_18.context: In 2 Kings 21:18, it is mentioned that Manasseh's son Amon succeeded him as king.

christianity_2_kings_21_11.meaning: Manasseh's wicked actions caused great sin in Judah, causing God's severe warning about judgement upon the people.
christianity_2_kings_21_11.context: This verse talks about King Manasseh of Judah who committed severe sins, following the evil practices of the Amorites before him and leading Judah to sin by worshipping idols.

christianity_2_kings_21_12.meaning: God declares judgement on Jerusalem and Judah because of Manasseh's evil deeds, causing fear among those hearing the prophecy.
christianity_2_kings_21_12.context: God speaks through His prophet, foretelling the calamities that will befall Jerusalem and Judah due to Manasseh's sins.

christianity_2_kings_21_13.meaning: God will punish Jerusalem by metaphorically measuring and destroying it, showing His displeasure.
christianity_2_kings_21_13.context: The verse describes God's plan to punish Jerusalem by using measuring tools (line and plummet) to symbolize judgement upon the city.

christianity_2_kings_21_14.meaning: God will abandon Judah, leading to their downfall and becoming a prey to their enemies.
christianity_2_kings_21_14.context: This verse talks about God turning away from the remaining people of Judah and allowing their enemies to conquer them and plunder their land.

christianity_2_kings_22_5.meaning: Resources should be used to repair and maintain places of worship, following proper oversight.
christianity_2_kings_22_5.context: The king asks workers to fix the temple, using money from the treasury.

christianity_2_kings_22_6.meaning: Every part of construction needs skilled people and proper materials to restore the sacred space.
christianity_2_kings_22_6.context: Workers are hired to build, cut stone, and buy timber for temple repairs.

christianity_2_kings_22_8.meaning: Discovering sacred texts reminds leaders to read and follow the law for guidance.
christianity_2_kings_22_8.context: High priest Hilkiah finds the law book in the temple and gives it to Shaphan.

christianity_2_kings_22_9.meaning: Transparency in spending shows accountability and keeps the temple’s work honest.
christianity_2_kings_22_9.context: Shaphan tells the king the money was spent on temple repairs by the workers.

christianity_2_kings_21_23.meaning: Bad actions often lead to terrible consequences. Trusting evil people usually brings harm and death to everyone involved.
christianity_2_kings_21_23.context: King Amon was betrayed by his own workers who killed him inside his royal home.

christianity_2_kings_21_24.meaning: Good people can rise up against evil. Choosing a wise leader helps restore peace and order to society.
christianity_2_kings_21_24.context: The citizens killed the traitors and chose young Josiah to be the new king of Judah.

christianity_2_kings_21_25.meaning: History records our deeds for future generations. We should learn from past mistakes to avoid repeating them.
christianity_2_kings_21_25.context: The writer refers readers to another historical book for more details about King Amon's life.

christianity_2_kings_21_26.meaning: Life continues after death. New leaders bring fresh starts and hope for a better future for all.
christianity_2_kings_21_26.context: Amon was buried in a garden tomb while his son Josiah took over the throne.

christianity_2_kings_22_1.meaning: God can use young people to lead with wisdom and faith if they trust in Him daily.
christianity_2_kings_22_1.context: Young Josiah became king of Judah at age eight and ruled for many years in Jerusalem.

christianity_2_kings_22_2.meaning: Living a good life means staying focused on God's path and avoiding wrong choices every single day.
christianity_2_kings_22_2.context: Josiah followed God's laws strictly and lived like his ancestor David without turning to bad habits.

christianity_2_kings_22_3.meaning: Leaders should delegate tasks to trustworthy people to ensure important work gets done correctly and on time.
christianity_2_kings_22_3.context: Years later, King Josiah sent his trusted scribe Shaphan to the temple to handle important religious duties.

christianity_2_kings_22_4.meaning: We should handle money with honesty and care when supporting our community or places of worship.
christianity_2_kings_22_4.context: Shaphan was told to meet the high priest to count the money people gave for temple repairs.

christianity_2_kings_22_10.meaning: The king learns the truth about the law, and the people must listen to God’s instructions.
christianity_2_kings_22_10.context: Shaphan the scribe tells King Josiah that priest Hilkiah brought a book, and Shaphan reads it.

christianity_2_kings_22_11.meaning: The king feels deep regret for his people’s disobedience and for the danger they face.
christianity_2_kings_22_11.context: After hearing the book’s words, King Josiah tears his clothes in sorrow.

christianity_2_kings_22_12.meaning: He wants the leaders to seek God’s guidance and follow His commands for Judah.
christianity_2_kings_22_12.context: The king orders Hilkiah, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asaiah to act on the book’s message.

christianity_2_kings_22_13.meaning: He urges them to seek God’s help because the nation faces serious consequences for ignoring His law.
christianity_2_kings_22_13.context: The king asks the leaders to ask God about the book’s words, warning of God’s anger.

christianity_2_kings_22_14.meaning: They sought guidance from a trusted prophet to understand God's message about the king's actions.
christianity_2_kings_22_14.context: Priests and officials went to prophetess Huldah in Jerusalem to ask about the book.

christianity_2_kings_22_15.meaning: God’s message would come through the official who requested it, showing His direct involvement.
christianity_2_kings_22_15.context: Huldah told them that God would speak to the man who sent them.

christianity_2_kings_22_16.meaning: The city would face punishment for its wrongdoings, and the king’s reading would be affected.
christianity_2_kings_22_16.context: God warned that He would bring trouble to the city and its people, including the book’s words.

christianity_2_kings_22_17.meaning: Their disobedience and idolatry would lead to God’s anger and lasting judgment on the place.
christianity_2_kings_22_17.context: God explained that the city would suffer because they worshiped other gods and defied Him.

christianity_2_kings_22_18.meaning: God answers the king, showing that He listens to those who seek His guidance.
christianity_2_kings_22_18.context: The king of Judah asks a prophet to speak to God about his questions.

christianity_2_kings_22_19.meaning: Humility and repentance bring comfort, but the prophet warns of future judgment for the land.
christianity_2_kings_22_19.context: The prophet speaks of the king’s humility and the sorrow of the people.

christianity_2_kings_22_20.meaning: Even in judgment, God promises peace and protection from seeing all evil.
christianity_2_kings_22_20.context: The prophet says God will bring peace after gathering the people to their graves.

christianity_2_kings_23_1.meaning: The king seeks wise counsel from leaders before deciding on the prophet’s words.
christianity_2_kings_23_1.context: The king gathers all elders of Judah and Jerusalem to hear the prophet’s message.

christianity_2_kings_23_2.meaning: Gathering together, they heard the covenant, reminding everyone of God’s promises and the need to follow His laws.
christianity_2_kings_23_2.context: The king, Judah people, priests, prophets, and all citizens gathered at Yahweh’s house to read the covenant book.

christianity_2_kings_23_3.meaning: He promised to obey God fully, showing devotion and commitment to living by God’s instructions.
christianity_2_kings_23_3.context: The king pledged before Yahweh to follow His commandments with all his heart and soul.

christianity_2_kings_23_4.meaning: He eliminated false worship, keeping the temple pure for worshiping only Yahweh.
christianity_2_kings_23_4.context: The king ordered the high priest to remove all Baal, Asherah, and other idol vessels from the temple.

christianity_2_kings_23_5.meaning: He stopped false religious practices, ensuring worship was directed only to Yahweh.
christianity_2_kings_23_5.context: The king removed idolatrous priests who burned incense to Baal, sun, moon, and other false gods.

christianity_2_kings_23_10.meaning: Us to protect children from being exploited for religious practices and to separate ourselves from evil idolatry.
christianity_2_kings_23_10.context: King Josiah of Judah prohibits child sacrifice to the false god Molech in Topheth, a valley near Jerusalem. He also removes horses dedicated to the sun god from the temple.

christianity_2_kings_23_11.meaning: The importance of purifying religious places and breaking idolatrous practices.
christianity_2_kings_23_11.context: King Josiah stops the worship of false gods by removing horses dedicated to the sun god from the temple courtyard. He orders the destruction of idols in the palace and temple.

christianity_2_kings_23_12.meaning: The significance of removing idolatry from sacred spaces and restoring righteousness.
christianity_2_kings_23_12.context: King Josiah cleanses the temple by destroying altars built by wicked kings Ahaz and Manasseh. He removes the altars dedicated to false gods.

christianity_2_kings_23_13.meaning: Us to reject and eliminate idolatry from our lives and communities, and to uphold true worship.
christianity_2_kings_23_13.context: King Josiah stops the worship of false gods Molech, Ashtoreth, and Chemosh in Jerusalem. He cleanses the city from these abominations.

christianity_2_kings_23_6.meaning: We must remove false worship from our lives and treat it as completely gone and useless.
christianity_2_kings_23_6.context: King Josiah removed a sacred wooden pole from the temple and burned it outside the city walls.

christianity_2_kings_23_7.meaning: We should clear out places and habits that lead us away from true and pure living.
christianity_2_kings_23_7.context: The king destroyed rooms used for immoral acts and where women made cloth for a false goddess.

christianity_2_kings_23_8.meaning: We must stop all wrong ways of worship and make sure only the right path remains.
christianity_2_kings_23_8.context: The king sent priests to ruin all the illegal worship spots built on hills across the land.

christianity_2_kings_23_9.meaning: Even when we lose a role, we can still share in the community and keep our bonds.
christianity_2_kings_23_9.context: Some priests stopped serving at the main altar but still ate bread with their fellow workers.

christianity_2_kings_23_22.meaning: The people had stopped following God’s special day, showing they forgot His rules.
christianity_2_kings_23_22.context: No Passover was kept since judges or kings until this time.

christianity_2_kings_23_23.meaning: Josiah restored God’s holy day, showing his commitment to obey God’s commands.
christianity_2_kings_23_23.context: In Josiah’s eighteenth year, the Passover was celebrated again in Jerusalem.

christianity_2_kings_23_24.meaning: He cleansed the land to follow God’s law, proving his devotion to true worship.
christianity_2_kings_23_24.context: Josiah removed spirits, wizards, idols, and other bad practices from Judah.

christianity_2_kings_23_25.meaning: Josiah’s sincere faith and obedience set a unique example for all future leaders.
christianity_2_kings_23_25.context: No king before or after matched Josiah’s wholehearted devotion to God.

christianity_2_kings_23_18.meaning: Us to respect the prophets and their messages, even if they are not accepted at first. It highlights the importance of honoring the sacred and following divine guidance.
christianity_2_kings_23_18.context: This verse is from the Christian Bible, specifically in the book of 2 Kings. It narrates an event during the reign of King Josiah, where he allows the bones of a prophet who warned the people but were not heeded to remain undisturbed.

christianity_2_kings_23_19.meaning: The importance of cleansing our lives and societies from idolatry and false worship practices, following the true teachings of our faith.
christianity_2_kings_23_19.context: King Josiah removes the pagan worship sites built by the wicked kings of Samaria to provoke God's anger.

christianity_2_kings_23_20.meaning: Us to purify ourselves from evil practices and follow the righteous path, as King Josiah did by destroying idolatry and upholding the true faith.
christianity_2_kings_23_20.context: The verse describes King Josiah's actions against the high places where idolatry took place, by destroying them and burning human bones on them.

christianity_2_kings_23_21.meaning: This verse encourages us to follow the commands of our faith and engage in religious practices that strengthen our connection with God, like celebrating the Passover.
christianity_2_kings_23_21.context: King Josiah issues a command for the people to celebrate the Passover festival as a way to honor God and keep His covenant.

christianity_2_kings_23_14.meaning: We must remove all false things from our lives to make room for true faith.
christianity_2_kings_23_14.context: King Josiah destroyed false worship items in the temple to clean it for God.

christianity_2_kings_23_15.meaning: We should tear down the bad habits and places that lead us away from God.
christianity_2_kings_23_15.context: The king destroyed the bad altar at Bethel that led many people to sin.

christianity_2_kings_23_16.meaning: God keeps His promises, and we must follow His instructions even when they seem strange.
christianity_2_kings_23_16.context: Josiah burned bones on the altar to fulfill an old prophecy about this specific place.

christianity_2_kings_23_17.meaning: We should listen to wise warnings from the past to avoid making the same mistakes.
christianity_2_kings_23_17.context: Locals told the king that this grave belonged to a prophet who warned about this altar.

christianity_2_kings_23_30.meaning: The people quickly chose a new king to keep the kingdom stable after a ruler's death.
christianity_2_kings_23_30.context: After King Josiah died, his son Jehoahaz was chosen and crowned king in Jerusalem.

christianity_2_kings_23_31.meaning: Short reigns show how fragile leadership can be when a king is young and inexperienced.
christianity_2_kings_23_31.context: Jehoahaz was only 23 and ruled for three months before his reign ended.

christianity_2_kings_23_32.meaning: Continuing wrong habits leads to trouble and shows the importance of learning from good examples.
christianity_2_kings_23_32.context: Jehoahaz followed his fathers' bad ways, doing things that angered God.

christianity_2_kings_23_33.meaning: Foreign powers can control a nation, reminding us that freedom can be lost if we do not protect our land.
christianity_2_kings_23_33.context: Egyptian Pharaoh held Jehoahaz captive and forced Israel to pay heavy tribute.

christianity_2_kings_23_34.meaning: Changing leaders without God's approval leads to loss and confusion for the people.
christianity_2_kings_23_34.context: Pharaoh replaced Josiah’s son with Jehoiakim, removed Jehoahaz, and Jehoahaz died in Egypt.

christianity_2_kings_23_35.meaning: Paying too much to outsiders hurts the nation and shows poor stewardship of resources.
christianity_2_kings_23_35.context: Jehoiakim gave gold and silver to Pharaoh and taxed the land to pay him.

christianity_2_kings_23_36.meaning: A king’s age and family background can influence how he governs and how people see him.
christianity_2_kings_23_36.context: Jehoiakim started ruling at twenty-five and reigned eleven years; his mother was Zebidah.

christianity_2_kings_23_37.meaning: Repeating bad habits brings God’s disapproval and harms the nation’s future.
christianity_2_kings_23_37.context: Jehoiakim did evil things that displeased God, following his fathers’ bad ways.

christianity_2_kings_23_26.meaning: Even good kings cannot fix all past sins. We must stay faithful every day to keep our hearts clean.
christianity_2_kings_23_26.context: God stayed angry at Judah because King Manasseh had done many bad things that made God very upset.

christianity_2_kings_23_27.meaning: Ignoring God leads to serious loss. We must value our relationship with him and not take his presence for granted.
christianity_2_kings_23_27.context: God promised to remove Judah from his sight just like he removed Israel because they broke their covenant with him.

christianity_2_kings_23_28.meaning: We should seek deeper knowledge of history and faith. Studying past stories helps us learn valuable lessons for today.
christianity_2_kings_23_28.context: The writer notes that more details about King Josiah are recorded in another historical book for those who want to read.

christianity_2_kings_23_29.meaning: Even brave leaders face death. We must trust God in dangerous times and accept that life is fragile and short.
christianity_2_kings_23_29.context: King Josiah fought against the Egyptian king at Megiddo and was killed during the battle while trying to stop him.

christianity_2_kings_24_5.meaning: Important historical records are kept in other books so we can learn more about past leaders.
christianity_2_kings_24_5.context: The writer points readers to another book for more details about King Jehoiakim's life and deeds.

christianity_2_kings_24_6.meaning: Life ends for everyone but leadership passes to the next generation to continue the work.
christianity_2_kings_24_6.context: King Jehoiakim died and was buried with his ancestors while his son Jehoiachin took the throne.

christianity_2_kings_24_7.meaning: Power shifts happen quickly and strong empires can take control of many lands and people.
christianity_2_kings_24_7.context: The king of Egypt stayed home because Babylon had conquered all the land from Egypt to Euphrates.

christianity_2_kings_24_8.meaning: Some leaders have very short reigns which shows how unstable and unpredictable political power can be.
christianity_2_kings_24_8.context: Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he started ruling and reigned for only three months in Jerusalem.

christianity_2_kings_24_9.meaning: Bad habits often pass from parents to children if we do not choose to do what is right.
christianity_2_kings_24_9.context: The new king followed his father's bad example and did wrong things that God hated very much.

christianity_2_kings_24_10.meaning: When we ignore warnings and live in sin, serious trouble often comes to knock at our door.
christianity_2_kings_24_10.context: Soldiers from the powerful Babylonian army arrived at Jerusalem and surrounded the city walls to cut off all help.

christianity_2_kings_24_11.meaning: Sometimes the consequences of our actions become so big that we must face them directly ourselves.
christianity_2_kings_24_11.context: The Babylonian king himself arrived to lead the attack while his troops continued to surround the city tightly.

christianity_2_kings_24_12.meaning: Pride and rebellion lead to loss of freedom, so we should stay humble and follow God's ways.
christianity_2_kings_24_12.context: The king of Judah surrendered with his family and officials, and the enemy captured them all quickly.

christianity_2_kings_24_1.meaning: Breaking your promises to those in power often leads to serious trouble and brings down judgment upon your own head.
christianity_2_kings_24_1.context: King Jehoiakim served Babylon for three years before he decided to rebel against the powerful king Nebuchadnezzar.

christianity_2_kings_24_2.meaning: When we ignore wise warnings and choose to do wrong, we must face the natural consequences of our bad choices.
christianity_2_kings_24_2.context: God sent various enemy armies to attack Judah because the people had disobeyed his clear warnings through the prophets.

christianity_2_kings_24_3.meaning: The bad actions of leaders can cause lasting harm to everyone, showing that our choices have long lasting effects.
christianity_2_kings_24_3.context: God allowed Judah to be removed from his sight because of the terrible sins committed by King Manasseh.

christianity_2_kings_24_4.meaning: Harming innocent people is a serious wrong that cannot be ignored, and justice will eventually catch up with us.
christianity_2_kings_24_4.context: King Manasseh filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, which was a grave sin that God would not forgive or overlook.

christianity_2_kings_24_13.meaning: God allowed this loss because the people broke their promises. It shows that ignoring God leads to losing blessings.
christianity_2_kings_24_13.context: The Babylonian king took gold treasures from the temple and the royal palace in Jerusalem.

christianity_2_kings_24_14.meaning: When a community turns away from good values, it loses its strength and best people quickly.
christianity_2_kings_24_14.context: The enemy took all the leaders, soldiers, and skilled workers away as prisoners from the city.

christianity_2_kings_24_15.meaning: Leaders must guide people well. Bad choices by leaders can bring trouble to their whole family.
christianity_2_kings_24_15.context: The king and his family were taken away to live in a foreign land far away.

christianity_2_kings_24_16.meaning: Strength and skill are useless if you do not follow wisdom. Humility is more important than power.
christianity_2_kings_24_16.context: Strong warriors and skilled workers were forced to leave their homes and go to Babylon.

christianity_2_kings_24_17.meaning: Powerful leaders can change rulers and names, showing how political forces shape history and control the fate of nations.
christianity_2_kings_24_17.context: The Babylonian king replaced the young ruler with his uncle and gave him a new royal name.

christianity_2_kings_24_18.meaning: Knowing a leader's age and reign length helps us understand the timeline of events and family connections in history.
christianity_2_kings_24_18.context: Zedekiah started ruling at age twenty-one and led the people of Jerusalem for eleven years total.

christianity_2_kings_24_19.meaning: Repeating the mistakes of others leads to failure, showing that we must choose to do what is right.
christianity_2_kings_24_19.context: Zedekiah acted wrongly in the eyes of God, following the same bad path as his predecessor Jehoiakim.

christianity_2_kings_24_20.meaning: Disobedience and rebellion bring serious consequences, reminding us that ignoring divine warnings leads to loss and suffering for everyone.
christianity_2_kings_24_20.context: God was angry with the people, so he removed them from his presence, and Zedekiah rebelled against Babylon.

christianity_2_kings_25_1.meaning: When we ignore God, serious consequences follow. We must stay faithful to avoid facing such overwhelming and dangerous trouble.
christianity_2_kings_25_1.context: King Nebuchadnezzar led his large army to surround Jerusalem and built strong forts around the city walls.

christianity_2_kings_25_2.meaning: Patience is hard during long trials. Trust God even when the situation feels hopeless and seems to last forever.
christianity_2_kings_25_2.context: The enemy army surrounded the city for a long time, keeping the people trapped inside without escape.

christianity_2_kings_25_3.meaning: Sin brings suffering to everyone. We should seek God early to avoid the pain of empty hands.
christianity_2_kings_25_3.context: Hunger became very bad in the city because there was no food left for the people.

christianity_2_kings_25_4.meaning: Running away from problems never works. Face your mistakes with courage and trust God for help.
christianity_2_kings_25_4.context: The walls broke, so the soldiers and king ran away at night through a secret gate.

christianity_2_kings_25_13.meaning: When we ignore God, we lose the special things that connect us to his holy presence.
christianity_2_kings_25_13.context: Soldiers destroyed the big bronze items in the temple and took them to Babylon.

christianity_2_kings_25_14.meaning: Disobedience leads to losing the simple tools we need to serve God with joy.
christianity_2_kings_25_14.context: The invaders took all the small tools used for daily worship in the temple.

christianity_2_kings_25_15.meaning: Pride and sin cause us to lose the precious gifts God gave us.
christianity_2_kings_25_15.context: The army leader took the valuable gold and silver items from the temple.

christianity_2_kings_25_16.meaning: The loss from turning away from God is often far greater than we can measure.
christianity_2_kings_25_16.context: The bronze from the huge pillars and sea was too much to weigh.

christianity_2_kings_25_9.meaning: Disobedience to God leads to the loss of sacred places and the destruction of what we value most.
christianity_2_kings_25_9.context: The enemy army set fire to the temple and royal palace in Jerusalem during their attack.

christianity_2_kings_25_10.meaning: When we ignore spiritual protection, our defenses fail and we become vulnerable to harm and danger.
christianity_2_kings_25_10.context: Soldiers from Babylon broke down the protective walls surrounding the city of Jerusalem completely.

christianity_2_kings_25_11.meaning: Sin brings consequences that remove us from our home and place us under foreign control.
christianity_2_kings_25_11.context: The army leader took the remaining people as prisoners to Babylon after the city fell.

christianity_2_kings_25_12.meaning: Even in judgment, God provides a way for survival and hope for those who remain.
christianity_2_kings_25_12.context: The commander allowed the poorest people to stay behind and work the land.

christianity_2_kings_25_5.meaning: Running away from your problems often leads to being caught. You cannot escape the consequences of your actions forever.
christianity_2_kings_25_5.context: The enemy army chased the fleeing king and caught him in the open fields near Jericho.

christianity_2_kings_25_6.meaning: Everyone must face the results of their choices. No one is above the law or justice.
christianity_2_kings_25_6.context: Soldiers took the captured king to the Babylonian ruler for a formal trial and judgment.

christianity_2_kings_25_7.meaning: Sin brings deep sorrow and loss. Bad choices can lead to painful and lasting consequences for you.
christianity_2_kings_25_7.context: The soldiers killed the king's sons in front of him and blinded him before taking him away.

christianity_2_kings_25_8.meaning: Time moves forward and events happen as planned. We must accept reality and face what comes.
christianity_2_kings_25_8.context: The Babylonian commander arrived in Jerusalem during the fifth month to carry out the final orders.

christianity_2_kings_25_17.meaning: Us about the importance of valuing and preserving ancient artifacts and historical structures. It also highlights the importance of maintaining the decorative elements on such structures.
christianity_2_kings_25_17.context: This verse describes a situation from the Bible, specifically in the book of 2 Kings. It talks about a tall pillar with a bronze capital on top, measuring 18 cubits in height. The capital had a bronze network and pomegranates around it.

christianity_2_kings_25_18.meaning: The importance of following orders from authority figures and the consequences of disobedience. It also highlights the significance of religious leaders and their roles in society.
christianity_2_kings_25_18.context: Specifically in the book of 2 Kings, the captain of the guard takes Seraiah, the chief priest, Zephaniah, the second priest, and three gatekeepers from the city.

christianity_2_kings_25_19.meaning: Us about the consequences of war and the impact it has on people's lives. It also highlights the roles of different people during times of conflict, such as the officer, the scribe, and the army captain.
christianity_2_kings_25_19.context: This verse from the Bible, found in the book of 2 Kings, describes the capture of Jerusalem by the Babylonians. It mentions six individuals taken from the city, including an officer, the scribe, and the captain of the army.

christianity_2_kings_25_20.meaning: The importance of following orders from authority figures and the possibility of mercy and compassion from those in power. It also highlights the significance of religious leaders and their protection during times of turmoil.
christianity_2_kings_25_20.context: Specifically in the book of 2 Kings, the Babylonian leader Nebuchadnezzar orders the destruction of the temple and other valuable items. However, the captain of the guard, Nebuzaradan, spares the lives of Seraiah, the chief priest, and the other priests.

christianity_2_kings_25_25.meaning: This verse tells the story of Ishmael and his men attacking Gedaliah, leading to his death and the suffering of Jews and Babylonians at Mizpah. It highlights the consequences of violence and betrayal.
christianity_2_kings_25_25.context: 2 Kings 25:25 - In the seventh month, Ishmael, a descendant of King Nebuchadnezzar, and ten men with him attacked Gedaliah, a governor appointed by the Babylonians, and killed him along with Jewish and Babylonian companions at Mizpah.

christianity_2_kings_25_26.meaning: This verse describes the fear that caused the people, including military leaders, to leave Judah and go to Egypt during a time of great distress.
christianity_2_kings_25_26.context: 2 Kings 25:26 - The people, including leaders, fled to Egypt due to fear of the Chaldeans after Jerusalem was destroyed.

christianity_2_kings_25_27.meaning: This verse tells the story of King Evilmerodach treating Jehoiachin with kindness after 37 years of imprisonment and giving him a higher position among Babylonian rulers.
christianity_2_kings_25_27.context: 2 Kings 25:27 - In the thirty-seventh year after Jehoiachin became a prisoner, King Evilmerodach of Babylon showed kindness to Jehoiachin and elevated his status among the other Babylonian kings.

christianity_2_kings_25_28.meaning: This verse explains that after capturing Jerusalem, the Babylonians took Jehoiachin and other prisoners to Babylon, where they were forced to work as farmers and laborers.
christianity_2_kings_25_28.context: 2 Kings 25:28 - The Babylonians took Jehoiachin and the other captives from Jerusalem to Babylon, where they became farmers and laborers.

christianity_2_kings_25_21.meaning: 2 Kings 25:21 - God allowed Nebuchadnezzar to punish Judah for their sins, causing many to suffer and be taken away from their homeland.
christianity_2_kings_25_21.context: 2 Kings 25:21 - King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon attacks Judah, killing many and taking Judah's people as captives.

christianity_2_kings_25_22.meaning: 2 Kings 25:22 - God uses Nebuchadnezzar to guide Gedaliah as a leader for the remaining people of Judah, showing mercy.
christianity_2_kings_25_22.context: 2 Kings 25:22 - Nebuchadnezzar appoints Gedaliah as a leader over the remaining people of Judah.

christianity_2_kings_25_23.meaning: 2 Kings 25:23 - Gedaliah reassures the people, promising safety if they stay in the land and serve Nebuchadnezzar, showing trust and unity.
christianity_2_kings_25_23.context: 2 Kings 25:23 - Gedaliah meets with a group of people including Ishmael, Johanan, and Seraiah.

christianity_2_kings_25_24.meaning: 2 Kings 25:24 - Gedaliah prevents a rebellion by encouraging the people to follow Nebuchadnezzar and maintain peace in the region.
christianity_2_kings_25_24.context: 2 Kings 25:24 - Gedaliah urges the people to stay in Judah and submit to Nebuchadnezzar, preventing a rebellion.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_7.meaning: These verses talk about the descendants of Japheth, Noah's son. Javan has four sons: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Rodanim. They are the origins of various people groups throughout history.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_7.context: These verses are from the book of 1 Chronicles in the Christian Bible. They mention the sons of Javan, a son of Japheth, who was one of the sons of Noah. The sons of Javan are Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Rodanim.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_8.meaning: These verses tell us about the children of Ham, Noah's son. Ham has four sons: Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan. These verses show the origins of different people groups from Ham's family.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_8.context: These verses also come from 1 Chronicles and discuss the sons of Ham, another son of Noah. Ham's sons are Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_9.meaning: This verse talks about the lineage of Cush, a son of Ham. Cush has five sons: Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca. Raamah has two sons: Sheba and Dedan. These verses explain the origins of different people groups from Cush's family.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_9.context: We learn about the descendants of Cush, a son of Ham. Cush has five sons: Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca. Raamah has two sons: Sheba and Dedan.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_10.meaning: These verses tell us about Nimrod, a descendant of Cush. Nimrod becomes a strong person and establishes the cities of Babylon, Bersabee, and Assyria. These verses show how people's families can influence history and the formation of nations.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_10.context: Verses 10-11 mention Nimrod, a grandson of Cush. Nimrod became a powerful person and founded the city of Babylon, Bersabee, and Assyria.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_3.meaning: Trust in God, live a long and meaningful life, and accept different perspectives in relationships.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_3.context: Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech were patriarchs in the Bible, mentioned in Christianity's Book of Genesis. Enoch walked with God and did not die, Methuselah lived the longest life, and Lamech took two wives.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_4.explanation:
This verse lists Noah and his three sons, who were the sole survivors of the Great Flood. They represent the ancestral foundation of humanity’s post-flood lineage.

Every individual is part of a larger historical and spiritual legacy. Recognizing your roots helps you understand your place in the broader human story.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_4.meaning: Every individual is part of a larger historical and spiritual legacy. Recognizing your roots helps you understand your place in the broader human story.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_4.context: This verse lists Noah and his three sons, who were the sole survivors of the Great Flood. They represent the ancestral foundation of humanity’s post-flood lineage.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_5.meaning: Diversity in family lineages leads to diverse cultures and nations.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_5.context: Japheth's sons in the Bible, mentioned in Christianity's Book of Genesis. They founded various nations and cultures.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_6.meaning: Descendants from different sons bring variety and formation of distinct groups.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_6.context: Gomer, Diphath, and Togarmah were sons of biblical patriarch Gomer in Christianity's Book of Genesis. They founded different tribes and peoples.

christianity_2_kings_25_29.meaning: Us that even in difficult situations, God can provide for our basic needs. King Jehoiachin was in prison, but he was still cared for by the king.
christianity_2_kings_25_29.context: This verse is from the Christian Bible, specifically in the book of 2 Kings. It talks about King Jehoiachin, who was imprisoned but still had access to the king's table and received food daily.

christianity_2_kings_25_30.meaning: Us that God provides for us daily, even when we face challenges or hardships. Jehoiachin received a constant allowance despite his situation.
christianity_2_kings_25_30.context: This verse is also from the Christian Bible, in the book of 2 Kings. It describes the daily provision given to Jehoiachin, the prisoner king, as a constant allowance from the king.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_1.meaning: The lineage of Adam's offspring, starting with Adam, then his son Seth, and finally Enosh. It emphasizes the continuity of human generations.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_1.context: This verse is from the Christian Bible, in the book of 1 Chronicles. It lists the generations of Adam's descendants starting with Adam, then Seth, and finally Enosh.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_2.meaning: This verse continues the lineage of Adam's offspring, starting with Kenan, then Mahalalel, and finally Jared. It highlights the passing of generations and the continuity of life.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_2.context: This verse is also from the Christian Bible, in the book of 1 Chronicles. It mentions the generations of Adam's descendants, starting with Kenan, then Mahalalel, and finally Jared.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_19.meaning: Names can tell us about big events, like how the world changed during Peleg's life.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_19.context: This verse lists the two sons of Eber, a man in the early human family tree.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_20.meaning: God uses ordinary people to build large families that spread across the whole earth.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_20.context: Joktan, the second son of Eber, had many children who started new family lines.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_21.meaning: Every person matters to God, even those whose names appear only briefly in history.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_21.context: This short list names three more sons of Joktan, continuing the record of his descendants.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_22.meaning: God cares about every single person, no matter how small their part in history seems.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_22.context: These are the final three sons of Joktan listed in this ancient family record.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_15.meaning: God kept track of every family line to show how all people are connected to Him.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_15.context: This list names three groups of people who were part of the ancient family records.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_16.meaning: Every person matters to God, so He recorded their names for all future generations.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_16.context: These are more names of ancient tribes listed in the genealogy of the early world.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_17.meaning: God used one family to start the human race again after the great flood.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_17.context: This verse lists the nine sons born to Shem, one of Noah's three sons.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_18.meaning: Life flows from one person to the next, showing God's steady plan for humanity.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_18.context: This shows the direct line of fathers and sons passing down through the generations.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_11.meaning: God created many different groups of people from one family, showing how all humans are connected.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_11.context: This list shows the sons of Mizraim, who was a son of Noah's son Ham.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_12.meaning: Even difficult neighbors came from the same human family, reminding us that everyone shares one origin.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_12.context: These are more sons of Mizraim, including the group that later became the Philistines.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_13.meaning: God gave each person a unique place in history, even if their ancestors made mistakes.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_13.context: Canaan, a son of Ham, had many sons, and Sidon was his very first child.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_14.meaning: All people are part of God's big plan, so we should treat every group with respect.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_14.context: These are other sons of Canaan, including groups who lived in the land of Canaan.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_23.meaning: It shows how God kept track of every family line to prove that all people are connected to Him.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_23.context: This verse lists the sons of Joktan, who was a descendant of Abraham through his son Keturah.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_24.meaning: It reminds us that God cares about every single person in history, not just the famous or powerful ones.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_24.context: These are the next three generations in the family tree of Shem, who was one of Noah's sons.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_25.meaning: It teaches that God's plan moves slowly but surely through many generations to bring about His great promises.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_25.context: This continues the list of ancestors leading down from Shem to Abraham, showing the unbroken chain of faith.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_26.meaning: It shows that God prepares the way for His chosen people by guiding their families step by step over time.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_26.context: These names lead directly to Terah, who was the father of Abraham, the great friend of God.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_27.meaning: God chose this man to start a great family that would bless all people.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_27.context: This verse names Abram, who later became Abraham, a key figure in the Bible.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_28.meaning: God kept His promise to Abraham by giving him children, even though he was old.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_28.context: Abraham had two sons, Isaac and Ishmael, from different women in his household.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_29.meaning: God cared for Ishmael and his family, showing that He watches over everyone.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_29.context: This list names the first sons of Ishmael, who was Abraham's son by Hagar.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_30.meaning: God multiplied Ishmael's descendants, proving that He fulfills His promises to all people.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_30.context: More names of Ishmael's sons are listed here to show his growing family line.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_31.meaning: God kept His promise to Abraham by giving him many descendants, even through his first son.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_31.context: This list names the children of Ishmael, who was Abraham's first son from another woman.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_32.meaning: God blessed Abraham with a large family, showing that His care extends to all his children.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_32.context: Abraham had a second wife named Keturah who gave birth to six sons and their children.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_33.meaning: Every person in this long family line is part of God's plan for the world.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_33.context: This verse lists the five sons of Midian, who was one of Keturah's children.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_34.meaning: God's special promise passed from father to son, leading to the chosen line of Israel.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_34.context: This short line connects Abraham to his son Isaac, and then to Isaac's two sons.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_35.meaning: God keeps careful records of every family line to show how all people are connected together.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_35.context: This list names the five sons born to Esau, who was Jacob's older brother.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_36.meaning: Every person matters to God, so He remembers each name and tracks their family history.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_36.context: Eliphaz was the first son of Esau, and this verse lists his seven children by name.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_37.meaning: God cares about every single person, even those who are not the main heroes of the story.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_37.context: Reuel was another son of Esau, and this verse lists the four sons he had.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_38.meaning: God knows the history of all nations and people, not just the chosen group of Israel.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_38.context: Seir was a local chief, and this verse lists the seven sons who came from his line.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_39.meaning: God keeps track of every person, showing that each individual life matters to Him.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_39.context: This verse lists the children of Lotan, a man who lived in the land of Edom.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_40.meaning: Every family has a place in history, and God sees the value in each person.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_40.context: The text names the sons of Shobal and Zibeon, who were leaders in the region of Edom.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_41.meaning: Our connections to others are important, and God cares about the bonds we share.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_41.context: This line traces the family tree of Anah and his son Dishon, who had four sons.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_42.meaning: No one is forgotten by God, and every name in history has a special purpose.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_42.context: The verse lists the children of Ezer and Dishan, continuing the record of Edom's families.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_43.meaning: Every nation has its own history and leaders. We should respect the past and learn from it.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_43.context: This lists the first rulers of Edom, a land near Israel, before Israel had its own kings.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_44.meaning: Leadership changes over time. New people step up to guide the community when old leaders pass away.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_44.context: After the first king died, his successor Jobab took the throne and ruled the people of Edom.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_45.meaning: Power moves from one person to another. Each leader brings their own style to guide the people.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_45.context: When Jobab died, Husham from the Teman region became the next king to rule over the land.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_46.meaning: Some leaders are strong fighters. They protect their people by standing up against outside threats.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_46.context: Hadad became king after Husham. He was a warrior who fought enemies in the fields of Moab.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_1.meaning: God remembers every person and family. Your roots matter because they connect you to a larger story of faith.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_1.context: This verse lists the first six sons of Jacob, who was also known as Israel.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_2.meaning: Every part of the community is important. No one is left out when God builds his family together.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_2.context: The list continues with the remaining six sons of Jacob, completing the twelve tribes of Israel.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_3.meaning: Bad choices have serious consequences. We must live righteously because God sees our actions clearly.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_3.context: Judah had three sons with a Canaanite woman. His firstborn son Er did evil and died.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_4.meaning: God can bring good from difficult situations. Life continues and grows even after tragedy strikes.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_4.context: Tamar gave birth to Perez and Zerah. Judah had five sons in total from these events.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_47.meaning: It shows that earthly power changes hands quickly. We should focus on eternal truths rather than temporary human rulers.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_47.context: This verse records the death of King Hadad and the start of Samlah's rule in Edom.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_48.meaning: Life is fleeting and leaders change. We must trust in God who remains constant through all times.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_48.context: Samlah passes away and Shaul takes his throne in the city of Rehoboth near the river.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_49.meaning: Human reigns are short. We should seek lasting spiritual values instead of chasing temporary worldly success or fame.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_49.context: Shaul dies and Baal Hanan becomes the next king of Edom in this historical record.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_50.meaning: God records every life detail. Our personal stories matter to Him even if they seem small to us.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_50.context: Hadad becomes king and the text notes his city name and his wife Mehetabel.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_51.meaning: The passage records the passing of a king and lists the chiefs who ruled after him, showing leadership succession.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_51.context: Hadad died, and the leaders of Edom were named: Timna, Aliah, and Jetheth.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_52.meaning: It continues the list of Edomite leaders, indicating the ongoing governance and family ties within the tribe.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_52.context: The next chiefs of Edom were Oholibamah, Elah, and Pinon.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_53.meaning: The text shows the continuity of authority, highlighting the importance of named leaders in the community's history.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_53.context: Further chiefs were Kenaz, Teman, and Mibzar, ruling over Edom.

christianity_1_chronicles_1_54.meaning: The passage concludes the record of Edomite chiefs, emphasizing the tribe's structured leadership and lineage.
christianity_1_chronicles_1_54.context: The final chiefs mentioned are Magdiel and Iram, completing the list of Edomite leaders.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_13.meaning: It shows that God often uses ordinary family lines to bring about great and important changes in history.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_13.context: This verse lists the first three sons born to Jesse, the father of King David.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_14.meaning: Every person in the family line matters, even if they are not the most famous or well known.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_14.context: The list continues with the names of the fourth and fifth sons of Jesse.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_15.meaning: God does not look at social rank or birth order, but chooses the humble heart for his work.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_15.context: David is named as the seventh son of Jesse, which was a low position in the family.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_16.meaning: Faith and strength can pass from one generation to the next through close family bonds and love.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_16.context: This mentions Jesse's daughters and the three brave sons of his daughter Zeruiah.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_5.meaning: It shows how God kept track of every family line to preserve the history of His chosen people.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_5.context: This verse lists the two sons born to Perez, who was a grandson of Jacob.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_6.meaning: Listing these names reminds us that God cares about every single person in the family of faith.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_6.context: Here we see the five sons of Zerah, who was a great-grandson of Jacob and part of Judah's line.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_7.meaning: This teaches us that hiding our sins brings trouble to the whole group, so we must always be honest.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_7.context: Achar, son of Carmi, is named here because he broke God's law by taking forbidden items from Jericho.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_8.meaning: It shows that God values every generation and keeps a careful record of who belongs to His family.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_8.context: This short verse simply records that Azariah was the son of Ethan, continuing the family record of Judah.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_9.meaning: It shows how God built a strong family line through ordinary men, preparing the way for future leaders.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_9.context: This verse lists the three sons born to Hezron, a key ancestor in the tribe of Judah.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_10.meaning: God uses steady, faithful families to raise up leaders who can guide His people with care and wisdom.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_10.context: Ram had a son named Amminadab, who then had a son named Nahshon, a leader of Judah.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_11.meaning: God works through generations, using kind and honest people to keep His promises alive and growing.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_11.context: Nahshon had a son named Salma, and Salma had a son named Boaz, a well-known biblical figure.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_12.meaning: This line leads to David, showing that God chooses humble people to do great things for His kingdom.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_12.context: Boaz had a son named Obed, and Obed had a son named Jesse, the father of King David.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_21.meaning: God can give new life and blessings even in the later years of your life.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_21.context: An older man named Hezron married a new wife and had a son named Segub.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_22.meaning: Your children can achieve great things and lead others if you raise them well.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_22.context: Segub had a son named Jair who ruled over many cities in the Gilead area.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_23.meaning: Things you work hard for can be lost, so do not put your hope in them.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_23.context: Enemy groups took away many cities that belonged to Jair and his family.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_24.meaning: Life continues and new people arrive even after the people we love pass away.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_24.context: After Hezron died, his wife gave birth to another son named Ashhur in a specific place.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_25.meaning: God keeps careful records of every family line to show how His people are connected across many generations.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_25.context: This lists the children of Jerahmeel, who was the first son of Hezron in the tribe of Judah.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_26.meaning: Every person has a unique place in the family tree, showing that no one is forgotten by God.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_26.context: Jerahmeel married a woman named Atarah, and she gave birth to a son named Onam for him.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_27.meaning: Leadership often passes from father to son, showing how responsibility and legacy are shared within families.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_27.context: Ram was the firstborn son of Jerahmeel, and he had three sons named Maaz, Jamin, and Eker.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_28.meaning: Life continues through the next generation, reminding us that our actions and faith impact those who come after us.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_28.context: Onam had two sons, Shammai and Jada. Shammai then had two sons of his own, Nadab and Abishur.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_17.meaning: God tracks every person in history, showing that each life has a place in the bigger story of His people.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_17.context: This verse lists the family line of Amasa, who was born to Abigail and a man named Jether.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_18.meaning: God blesses families with many children, showing that He cares about the growth and continuity of His chosen people.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_18.context: Caleb, a famous leader, had several sons from his first wife, Azubah, and another woman named Jerioth.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_19.meaning: Life moves forward even after loss, as God provides new companions and continues to bless families with new generations.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_19.context: After his first wife died, Caleb married a new woman named Ephrath, and she gave birth to a son named Hur.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_20.meaning: Every generation passes the faith and legacy to the next, showing that God's work continues through ordinary family lines.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_20.context: This short line connects Hur to his son Uri, and then Uri to his son Bezalel in the family tree.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_37.meaning: Each generation passes on family names and responsibilities to the next person.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_37.context: Zabad had a son named Ephlal, and Ephlal had a son named Obed.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_38.meaning: Family lines continue, showing how people are connected through parents and children.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_38.context: Obed had a son named Jehu, and Jehu had a son named Azariah.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_39.meaning: The story reminds us that our family history is built one generation at a time.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_39.context: Azariah had a son named Helez, and Helez had a son named Eleasah.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_40.meaning: Each new generation keeps the family story alive and teaches future people.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_40.context: Eleasah had a son named Sismai, and Sismai had a son named Shallum.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_29.meaning: Family names show lineage and the importance of recording ancestry for future generations.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_29.context: Abishur's wife Abihail had two sons, Ahban and Molid, in ancient Israel.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_30.meaning: Even in families, some lines end, reminding us that life can be unpredictable.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_30.context: Nadab had two sons, Seled and Appaim; Seled died childless.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_31.meaning: Generations link people together, showing how family stories pass down through time.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_31.context: Appaim's son Ishi had a son Sheshan, who had a son Ahlai.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_32.meaning: Not all family lines continue, highlighting the fragility and value of each life.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_32.context: Jada, brother of Shammai, had sons Jether and Jonathan; Jether died childless.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_33.meaning: This verse is about the family tree of King David's son Jonathan. Peleth and Zaza were his sons, and their father was Jerahmeel.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_33.context: In the Bible, this verse talks about the lineage of King David. It mentions the sons of Jonathan, one of David's sons, named Peleth and Zaza, and their father Jerahmeel.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_34.meaning: The verse is from the Bible's Chronicles book and discusses Sheshan, who had only daughters but later married one of them to his Egyptian servant, Jarha.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_34.context: This verse is from the Bible's book of Chronicles and talks about Sheshan, who had only daughters but later gave one of them in marriage to his servant Jarha, an Egyptian.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_35.meaning: The verse is from the Bible's Chronicles book and tells the story of Sheshan giving his daughter to Jarha, his servant, in marriage. Jarha and his son Attai become the parents of Nathan.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_35.context: In this Bible verse, Sheshan gives his daughter to Jarha, his servant, as a wife. Jarha and his son Attai become the parents of Nathan.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_36.meaning: The verse continues the family tree story from the Bible's Chronicles book, stating that Attai is the father of Zabad.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_36.context: This verse from the Bible's Chronicles book continues the family tree story, mentioning that Attai is the father of Zabad.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_49.meaning: God remembers every person in history, showing that each life matters and has a specific role to play.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_49.context: This verse lists the children of Caleb, a brave leader who helped Israel enter the promised land.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_50.meaning: Our ancestors built communities that last, reminding us to create lasting good things for future generations.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_50.context: The text identifies Shobal as a son of Caleb and the founder of a specific ancient town.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_51.meaning: God uses ordinary people to start important places, showing that humble beginnings can lead to great things.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_51.context: This line names two men who started the towns of Bethlehem and Beth Gader in the region.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_52.meaning: We are all connected to a larger family, and our actions affect the whole group we belong to.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_52.context: Shobal had a son named Haroeh who was part of a group called the Menuhoth.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_45.meaning: God tracks every family line to show that each person has a special place in His big plan.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_45.context: This verse lists the family line of Shammai, showing how his son Maon started a new branch.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_46.meaning: God cares about all people, even those in less formal roles, and gives them important roles in history.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_46.context: Ephah, a woman in Caleb's household, had three sons who became part of the tribe of Judah.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_47.meaning: God blesses families with many children, showing that growth and community are part of His good design.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_47.context: This short list names the six sons of a man named Jahdai, showing his family grew quite large.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_48.meaning: Every person is valued by God, and even smaller family branches contribute to the whole story of faith.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_48.context: Maacah, another woman in Caleb's home, gave birth to two sons who joined the family record.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_41.meaning: It shows how God's people were connected through generations, keeping their history and identity safe.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_41.context: This verse lists the direct family line of a man named Shallum and his descendants.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_42.meaning: It reminds us that every person in the family tree has a place and a purpose in God's plan.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_42.context: This part describes the children of Caleb, who was the brother of another man named Jerahmeel.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_43.meaning: Listing these names honors the family and shows that God cares about every single individual.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_43.context: Here we see the names of the four sons born to a man named Hebron.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_44.meaning: It teaches us that our actions and lives are part of a larger story that lasts for many years.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_44.context: This verse continues the family record by showing the children of Shema and Rekem.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_53.meaning: God keeps track of every family line to show how His people are connected and preserved over time.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_53.context: This list names specific family groups that lived in a town called Kiriath Jearim in ancient Israel.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_54.meaning: Every person has a role in the bigger picture, and God values each individual and their family line.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_54.context: This verse lists the children of Salma and the various towns and groups they led or represented.

christianity_1_chronicles_2_55.meaning: Knowledge and wisdom are passed down through generations, and we should honor those who preserve truth.
christianity_1_chronicles_2_55.context: This describes scribes living in Jabez and connects them to the Kenites, a group with a long history.

christianity_1_chronicles_3_1.meaning: God uses ordinary family moments to build His plan, and every child is part of a larger divine story.
christianity_1_chronicles_3_1.context: This lists the first two sons born to King David while he was ruling from the city of Hebron.

christianity_1_chronicles_3_2.meaning: Knowing who your family is helps you understand your roots and the people around you.
christianity_1_chronicles_3_2.context: This list names two of King David's sons, showing their mothers and royal family ties.

christianity_1_chronicles_3_3.meaning: Every person has a unique place in the family story, and each one matters.
christianity_1_chronicles_3_3.context: The text continues listing David's sons, naming two more and identifying their specific mothers.

christianity_1_chronicles_3_4.meaning: Life changes as we grow, and we must be ready to move to new places.
christianity_1_chronicles_3_4.context: David had six sons in Hebron and ruled there for a short time before moving.

christianity_1_chronicles_3_5.meaning: God often uses specific people and moments to guide the future of a family or nation.
christianity_1_chronicles_3_5.context: David had four sons in Jerusalem, including Solomon, who was born to his wife Bathsheba.

christianity_1_chronicles_3_6.meaning: It shows that God kept careful records of every person in the royal family line.
christianity_1_chronicles_3_6.context: This list names three of King David's sons born to his wife Bathsheba.

christianity_1_chronicles_3_7.meaning: Every person matters to God, so even simple names are preserved in history.
christianity_1_chronicles_3_7.context: These are more names of David's children, continuing the list of his family members.

christianity_1_chronicles_3_8.meaning: God values order and truth, so counting helps us understand the full picture.
christianity_1_chronicles_3_8.context: The text counts the total number of sons David had from his main wives.

christianity_1_chronicles_3_9.meaning: God includes everyone in his plan, showing that no one is left out of his care.
christianity_1_chronicles_3_9.context: This verse notes that David had other children from concubines and a sister named Tamar.

christianity_1_chronicles_3_10.meaning: God kept His promise to David by giving his family a long line of rulers over Israel.
christianity_1_chronicles_3_10.context: This list shows the kings who ruled after Solomon, starting with his son Rehoboam.

christianity_1_chronicles_3_11.meaning: History records how power passed from father to son, showing the steady flow of leadership.
christianity_1_chronicles_3_11.context: The genealogy continues with more kings who ruled the kingdom of Judah in succession.

christianity_1_chronicles_3_12.meaning: Every person in this line matters, showing that God cares about each individual in history.
christianity_1_chronicles_3_12.context: More names are listed to track the royal family line through several generations of kings.

christianity_1_chronicles_3_13.meaning: Even when kings made mistakes, God remained faithful to His chosen people and their future.
christianity_1_chronicles_3_13.context: The list ends with Manasseh, a king who ruled for a long time in Judah.

christianity_1_chronicles_3_18.meaning: God keeps track of every person in history, showing that no one is forgotten or unimportant.
christianity_1_chronicles_3_18.context: This list names six men who were part of the royal family of Judah.

christianity_1_chronicles_3_19.meaning: God uses ordinary families to carry out his big plans and restore his people to their land.
christianity_1_chronicles_3_19.context: This verse lists the children of Pedaiah, including Zerubbabel, who led the return from exile.
