christianity_ezra_2_68.meaning: This verse shows the dedication and generosity of these individuals who contributed to the rebuilding of the temple. It teaches us the importance of supporting religious and spiritual causes and being generous towards them.
christianity_ezra_2_68.context: We learn about some of the heads of fathers' households who came to Jerusalem. These individuals contributed to the temple's construction by giving gold, silver, and priestly garments.

christianity_ezra_2_69.meaning: The importance of prioritizing spiritual matters over material possessions. Despite having many animals, these people focused on rebuilding Jerusalem and serving God.
christianity_ezra_2_69.context: This verse is also from the book of Ezra. It mentions the number of camels and donkeys owned by the same people who returned to Jerusalem. Again, this verse is part of a list of animals and their respective numbers.

christianity_ezra_3_8.meaning: God wants us to begin important work with the right leaders and a clear plan.
christianity_ezra_3_8.context: The returned people started building the new temple in Jerusalem two years after their arrival.

christianity_ezra_3_9.meaning: God gives specific roles to people so that every part of the work is done well.
christianity_ezra_3_9.context: Priests and Levites were chosen to lead the workers and manage the construction of the temple.

christianity_ezra_3_10.meaning: We should celebrate God's presence and thank him when we start new projects or steps.
christianity_ezra_3_10.context: As the foundation stones were placed, priests played trumpets and Levites played cymbals to praise God.

christianity_ezra_3_11.meaning: God's love is always with his people, and we should show joy in his faithfulness.
christianity_ezra_3_11.context: The crowd sang songs of praise and shouted loudly because the temple foundation was finally laid.

christianity_ezra_4_3.meaning: Sometimes you must set clear boundaries to protect your sacred goals from outside interference or mixed motives.
christianity_ezra_4_3.context: The returned Jews told their neighbors they could not help build the new temple for their God.

christianity_ezra_4_4.meaning: People who oppose your good work will often try to make you feel weak or give up on your mission.
christianity_ezra_4_4.context: Local residents tried to stop the Jewish builders by discouraging them and causing trouble during the construction work.

christianity_ezra_4_5.meaning: Evil plans can drag on for a long time, but your faith should keep you moving forward despite delays.
christianity_ezra_4_5.context: Opponents paid lawyers to block the temple project for many years across different Persian kings' reigns.

christianity_ezra_4_6.meaning: When you face unfair attacks, remember that truth and patience are stronger than false accusations written by others.
christianity_ezra_4_6.context: During a new king's early rule, enemies wrote a formal complaint against the people living in Jerusalem.

christianity_ezra_3_12.meaning: We can feel both sadness for the past and deep happiness for the present at the same time.
christianity_ezra_3_12.context: Older men who remembered the first temple cried sadly while others shouted with great joy.

christianity_ezra_3_13.meaning: Strong emotions can mix together so loudly that it is hard to separate the different feelings.
christianity_ezra_3_13.context: The crowd made so much noise that people could not tell the crying from the cheering.

christianity_ezra_4_1.meaning: When we start a good project, others who oppose us will often notice and react quickly.
christianity_ezra_4_1.context: Enemies of the Jewish people heard that the returned captives were building a new temple.

christianity_ezra_4_2.meaning: People may offer help with false motives, so we must carefully check their true intentions.
christianity_ezra_4_2.context: The enemies asked to help build the temple, claiming they worshipped the same God for years.

christianity_ezra_4_11.meaning: People often use official channels to report problems, but sometimes these reports are based on fear and jealousy.
christianity_ezra_4_11.context: Enemies of the Jews wrote a formal letter to the Persian king to complain about their rebuilding efforts.

christianity_ezra_4_12.meaning: Opponents often exaggerate or twist the truth to make good actions look like dangerous threats to power.
christianity_ezra_4_12.context: The letter claimed the returning Jews were rebuilding Jerusalem and finishing the city walls in a rebellious way.

christianity_ezra_4_13.meaning: Fear of losing control or money can make people oppose progress, even when that progress is good for everyone.
christianity_ezra_4_13.context: They warned the king that a rebuilt city would stop paying taxes and cause financial loss to the empire.

christianity_ezra_4_14.meaning: People may claim loyalty to justify their actions, but true loyalty should not mean spreading lies or causing harm.
christianity_ezra_4_14.context: The writers said they owed loyalty to the king and felt it was their duty to report this issue.

christianity_ezra_4_7.meaning: People used official channels to report on events, showing how power structures controlled daily life.
christianity_ezra_4_7.context: Some men wrote a formal letter to the Persian king about the rebuilding of Jerusalem.

christianity_ezra_4_8.meaning: Leaders sometimes use their positions to block progress, reminding us to stand firm in good work.
christianity_ezra_4_8.context: Two high-ranking officials drafted a complaint letter to the king about the Jewish builders.

christianity_ezra_4_9.meaning: Many different people can join together to oppose a shared goal, so unity is important.
christianity_ezra_4_9.context: The letter listed many different groups of people who lived in the region of Samaria.

christianity_ezra_4_10.meaning: History shapes who lives where, and understanding the past helps us see current conflicts clearly.
christianity_ezra_4_10.context: These groups were originally moved to the area by a previous king to settle the land.

christianity_ezra_4_15.meaning: People often use past mistakes to stop others from doing good things today.
christianity_ezra_4_15.context: Enemies told the king to check old records about Jerusalem being a place of past trouble.

christianity_ezra_4_16.meaning: Selfish people use fear of loss to stop progress and keep power for themselves.
christianity_ezra_4_16.context: They warned the king that rebuilding the city would cost him land and tax money.

christianity_ezra_4_17.meaning: Leaders respond to reports and accusations from people who want to control others.
christianity_ezra_4_17.context: The king sent a reply to the officials in Samaria who had written the complaint letter.

christianity_ezra_4_18.meaning: When leaders hear complaints, they pay close attention to the details presented to them.
christianity_ezra_4_18.context: The king told them that he had read their letter clearly and understood their claims.

christianity_ezra_5_3.meaning: The concern of local officials about a mysterious construction project. They sought the origin of the decree to rebuild the temple and finish the wall, trying to find out who authorized it.
christianity_ezra_5_3.context: This verse talks about Tattenai, the governor beyond the River, and Shetharbozenai along with their companions who questioned Ezra's team about the authority to rebuild the temple and complete the wall in Jerusalem. They wanted to know who gave the decree for this construction project.

christianity_ezra_5_4.meaning: This verse describes the officials' curiosity about the individuals contributing to the temple reconstruction and wall completion project.
christianity_ezra_5_4.context: The officials inquired about the names of the people involved in the building work.

christianity_ezra_5_5.meaning: This verse explains that the Lord provided protection for the Jews while they worked on rebuilding the temple and completing the wall. Their efforts continued until their matter reached King Darius, who then provided a response.
christianity_ezra_5_5.context: The Lord watched over the Jews to protect them and not stop them until their request reached King Darius and a response was received.

christianity_ezra_5_6.meaning: This verse tells us about Tattenai, the governor beyond the River, and Shetharbozenai and their companions who wrote a letter to King Darius regarding the construction project.
christianity_ezra_5_6.context: Tattenai, the governor beyond the River, and Shetharbozenai, along with their companions, sent a letter to King Darius.

christianity_ezra_4_23.meaning: The verse teaches us to respect authority and follow laws. When faced with opposition, we should seek peaceful solutions rather than using force. It also highlights the importance of obeying kings and their commands.
christianity_ezra_4_23.context: This verse describes a situation where Rehum, Shimshai the scribe, and their companions read a letter from King Artaxerxes of Persia to the Jews in Jerusalem. They used force to stop the work on the temple being rebuilt. The verse takes place during the time when Ezra the scribe is leading the Jewish community.

christianity_ezra_4_24.meaning: The verse emphasizes patience and persistence in the face of adversity. It shows that God is with those who seek to serve Him and follow His will.
christianity_ezra_4_24.context: This verse continues the story from verse 1. Work on the temple stopped for the second year of King Darius' reign due to opposition from enemies. The Jews continued to rebuild the temple under God's guidance.

christianity_ezra_5_1.meaning: The verse highlights the importance of faith, unity, and following God's guidance. It encourages us to seek wisdom from spiritual leaders and work together towards a common goal.
christianity_ezra_5_1.context: This verse introduces Haggai and Zechariah as prophets who encouraged the Jews to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem. Zerubbabel and Jeshua, the leaders, started the construction with the help of the prophets.

christianity_ezra_5_2.meaning: The verse teaches us to stay determined in the face of adversity and to seek support from spiritual leaders and fellow believers. It demonstrates the importance of perseverance and unity in fulfilling God's will.
christianity_ezra_5_2.context: Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the prophets continued to rebuild the temple despite opposition from their enemies. The people remained committed to their task.

christianity_ezra_4_19.meaning: The city's past behavior of defying authority and causing chaos. It highlights the importance of following laws and respecting rulers.
christianity_ezra_4_19.context: This verse talks about a search conducted regarding a city that has rebelled against kings in the past and caused trouble. It mentions the city's history of insurrection, rebellion, and revolts.

christianity_ezra_4_20.meaning: This verse talks about the history of strong leaders governing the region and the people submitting to their authority by paying taxes and following their rules.
christianity_ezra_4_20.context: The verse mentions that powerful kings have ruled over Jerusalem and the surrounding area, and the people living there paid tribute, custom, and toll to them.

christianity_ezra_4_21.meaning: This verse advises the leaders to follow divine guidance and delay the city's development until they receive further instructions from their higher authority.
christianity_ezra_4_21.context: God instructs the leaders to issue a decree stopping the construction of the city until further instructions are received from Him.

christianity_ezra_4_22.meaning: This verse encourages the leaders to take action based on divine instructions and to think about the possible negative outcomes for themselves and the community if they neglect their responsibilities.
christianity_ezra_4_22.context: The verse warns the leaders to not be lazy in following God's command and to consider the potential consequences for themselves and the people.

christianity_ezra_5_15.meaning: We should look for past promises and records to confirm what is right and true.
christianity_ezra_5_15.context: The Persian governor tells the Jewish leaders to find the old royal decree in the archives.

christianity_ezra_5_16.meaning: Important work can stall for a long time, but it still needs to be finished.
christianity_ezra_5_16.context: The Jews started building the temple long ago, but the work has stopped for many years.

christianity_ezra_5_17.meaning: We should verify facts and check history before making big decisions or judgments.
christianity_ezra_5_17.context: The governor asks the king to check old records to see if the building was allowed.

christianity_ezra_6_1.meaning: Leaders must take action to find the truth and support what is right and just.
christianity_ezra_6_1.context: King Darius orders his officials to search the royal archives in Babylon for the old decree.

christianity_ezra_5_7.meaning: People in power often check on projects to make sure they follow the rules and laws.
christianity_ezra_5_7.context: Local leaders wrote a formal letter to King Darius to report on the Jewish rebuilding efforts.

christianity_ezra_5_8.meaning: Hard work and dedication can make big projects grow quickly and look very impressive to others.
christianity_ezra_5_8.context: The letter described the temple being built with strong stones and wood, showing fast progress.

christianity_ezra_5_9.meaning: It is important to have proper authority and permission before starting any major new project.
christianity_ezra_5_9.context: The officials asked the Jewish elders who gave them the official permission to start building the temple.

christianity_ezra_5_10.meaning: Knowing who is in charge helps leaders make fair decisions and keep track of responsibilities.
christianity_ezra_5_10.context: The officials wanted the names of the leaders so they could report them to the king.

christianity_ezra_5_11.meaning: We proudly state who we serve and why we are working hard to restore our sacred place of worship.
christianity_ezra_5_11.context: The Jewish leaders told the officials they serve the true God and are rebuilding the old temple.

christianity_ezra_5_12.meaning: When we turn away from God, we face serious consequences, and our community can be broken and scattered.
christianity_ezra_5_12.context: The people told how their ancestors angered God, leading to their defeat and capture by the Babylonian king.

christianity_ezra_5_13.meaning: God can use powerful rulers to open doors for his people, even when they seem to be against them.
christianity_ezra_5_13.context: King Cyrus of Babylon issued an official order allowing the Jewish people to rebuild their temple in Jerusalem.

christianity_ezra_5_14.meaning: God ensures that what was stolen from his house is returned, showing that he cares deeply about his worship.
christianity_ezra_5_14.context: Cyrus returned the stolen gold and silver items that the Babylonians had taken from the temple in Jerusalem.

christianity_ezra_6_2.meaning: Checking past records helps us find the truth and solve problems that seem stuck or confusing.
christianity_ezra_6_2.context: Officials searched old palace records in Media to find proof about the temple building project.

christianity_ezra_6_3.meaning: God can use powerful leaders to help his people return home and start fresh again.
christianity_ezra_6_3.context: King Cyrus allowed the Jewish people to rebuild their holy temple in Jerusalem after a long exile.

christianity_ezra_6_4.meaning: God provides the resources we need to build strong and lasting things in our lives.
christianity_ezra_6_4.context: The king ordered that the temple be built with strong stones and wood using royal funds.

christianity_ezra_6_5.meaning: Restoring what was taken helps heal past wounds and brings things back to where they belong.
christianity_ezra_6_5.context: The king ordered that stolen temple items be returned to Jerusalem from Babylon to their proper place.

christianity_ezra_6_6.meaning: Leaders must step back and let people finish their important work without unnecessary blocking.
christianity_ezra_6_6.context: The king orders the local governor to stop interfering with the Jewish builders right away.

christianity_ezra_6_7.meaning: We should support others in restoring what is broken and help them build a better future.
christianity_ezra_6_7.context: The royal decree tells the governor to let the Jewish elders rebuild their temple in its original spot.

christianity_ezra_6_8.meaning: Generous funding helps communities build strong places for worship and shared spiritual life together.
christianity_ezra_6_8.context: The king commands that tax money from the region be used to pay for the temple construction costs.

christianity_ezra_6_9.meaning: Consistent care and provision show deep respect for spiritual traditions and the needs of the faithful.
christianity_ezra_6_9.context: The order requires daily supplies of animals and food for the priests to offer sacrifices to God.

christianity_ezra_6_10.meaning: We should show gratitude to God and pray for leaders so they can protect and guide us well.
christianity_ezra_6_10.context: The king ordered priests to offer sacrifices and pray for the royal family's safety and long life.

christianity_ezra_6_11.meaning: God takes his commands seriously, so we must respect authority and not try to change divine instructions.
christianity_ezra_6_11.context: The king issued a harsh warning that anyone changing this order would face severe physical punishment and shame.

christianity_ezra_6_12.meaning: No human power can stop God's plans, so we should trust him to protect his holy work.
christianity_ezra_6_12.context: Darius declared that God would punish any ruler who tried to stop the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem.

christianity_ezra_6_13.meaning: When we hear God's direction, we should act quickly and obey with a willing and eager heart.
christianity_ezra_6_13.context: The local governors quickly followed the king's orders to help rebuild the temple without any delay or resistance.

christianity_ezra_6_18.meaning: Understanding and following written instructions ensures orderly and sacred ceremonies.
christianity_ezra_6_18.context: The people arrange priests and Levites for their duties during a religious event in Jerusalem, following the instructions in the book of Moses.

christianity_ezra_6_19.meaning: Following religious traditions and maintaining connections with one's heritage is important.
christianity_ezra_6_19.context: The Jewish exiles celebrate the Passover on the right date according to their sacred calendar.

christianity_ezra_6_20.explanation:
The Jewish priests and Levites underwent ritual purification to prepare for the Passover celebration. They performed the sacrifice on behalf of the Israelites who had returned from Babylonian exile.

Spiritual preparation and communal unity are essential before approaching sacred duties. True worship requires a clean heart and a collective commitment to honoring God's established traditions.
christianity_ezra_6_20.meaning: Spiritual preparation and communal unity are essential before approaching sacred duties. True worship requires a clean heart and a collective commitment to honoring God's established traditions.
christianity_ezra_6_20.context: The Jewish priests and Levites underwent ritual purification to prepare for the Passover celebration. They performed the sacrifice on behalf of the Israelites who had returned from Babylonian exile.

christianity_ezra_6_21.meaning: Separating from worldly influences and seeking spiritual connection brings unity and purity.
christianity_ezra_6_21.context: The returning exiles and those who separated from pagan practices join together to worship Yahweh, showing their desire to connect with their faith.

christianity_ezra_6_14.meaning: Following divine inspiration and rulers' decisions can lead to successful completion of important projects.
christianity_ezra_6_14.context: The rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem continues as the Jewish elders receive guidance from Haggai and Zechariah. They follow God's command and Cyrus, Darius, and King Ahasuerus' decree.

christianity_ezra_6_15.meaning: Patience and persistence pay off as the temple is rebuilt after a six-year period.
christianity_ezra_6_15.context: The temple is finished on Adar 3, year 6 of Darius the king. This event marks a significant milestone in the temple's restoration.

christianity_ezra_6_16.meaning: Community unity and shared joy result from accomplishing a sacred task together.
christianity_ezra_6_16.context: The temple's dedication brings joy to the Jewish community, including priests, Levites, and other exiles returning from Babylon.

christianity_ezra_6_17.meaning: Sacrifices and repentance unite the community and demonstrate their commitment to God.
christianity_ezra_6_17.context: During the dedication ceremony, they offer numerous animals as sacrifices to atone for the sins of the people, representing their repentance.

christianity_ezra_6_22.meaning: Us to be grateful for our blessings and attribute them to God's guidance. It also highlights the importance of unity and cooperation in accomplishing God's work.
christianity_ezra_6_22.context: This verse is from the Christian book of Ezra, describing the celebration of unleavened bread feast by the people of Israel after their success in rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem. The king of Assyria supported their efforts and their joy was due to God's intervention.

christianity_ezra_7_1.meaning: This verse establishes Ezra's background and the context of his journey to Jerusalem. It emphasizes the importance of following one's calling and serving God, even in distant lands.
christianity_ezra_7_1.context: This verse introduces the story of Ezra, a priest and scribe, who received a letter from the Persian king Artaxerxes to help rebuild the temple in Jerusalem. Ezra is from the lineage of the priest Ahitub.

christianity_ezra_7_2.meaning: This verse continues Ezra's lineage and highlights the priestly role he inherited. It emphasizes the importance of passing on religious knowledge and traditions from generation to generation.
christianity_ezra_7_2.context: Ezra's lineage continues with his father Seraiah, who was a priest and scribe. His ancestor Ahitub was the high priest.

christianity_ezra_7_3.meaning: This verse continues Ezra's lineage and showcases the dedication to religious roles within his family. It emphasizes the significance of dedicating one's life to serving God and upholding religious teachings.
christianity_ezra_7_3.context: Ezra's lineage further extends to his grandfather Azariah, who was also a priest and scribe. His ancestor Meraioth was a high priest.

christianity_ezra_7_4.meaning: Knowing your roots helps you understand who you are and where you truly come from.
christianity_ezra_7_4.context: This verse lists the family line of Ezra, showing his direct ancestors in order.

christianity_ezra_7_5.meaning: Your heritage connects you to a long history of faith and service to God.
christianity_ezra_7_5.context: The list continues back to Aaron, the first high priest chosen by God long ago.

christianity_ezra_7_6.meaning: When you prepare well and trust God, even powerful leaders will support your good work.
christianity_ezra_7_6.context: Ezra traveled from Babylon to Jerusalem because he knew God's laws well and the king helped him.

christianity_ezra_7_7.meaning: Working together as a united group makes it much easier to finish big and important tasks.
christianity_ezra_7_7.context: Many different groups of people traveled together to return to Jerusalem and rebuild their holy place.

christianity_ezra_7_12.meaning: God uses powerful leaders to help His people, showing that even kings can serve a higher purpose.
christianity_ezra_7_12.context: The Persian king writes a letter to Ezra, a priest, to start his official mission.

christianity_ezra_7_13.meaning: True service comes from a willing heart, not from being forced, and God values free choice.
christianity_ezra_7_13.context: The king allows any willing Israelite, priest, or Levite to travel with Ezra to Jerusalem.

christianity_ezra_7_14.meaning: Leaders should follow God's rules and care for the well-being of the community they serve.
christianity_ezra_7_14.context: Ezra is sent by the king and his advisors to check on the people and their laws.

christianity_ezra_7_15.meaning: Generous giving supports worship and shows that resources should be shared for God's house.
christianity_ezra_7_15.context: The king gives silver and gold freely to be brought to the temple in Jerusalem.

christianity_ezra_7_8.meaning: God guides his people at the right time, even when they return to their home.
christianity_ezra_7_8.context: Ezra arrived in Jerusalem during the seventh year of the king's rule.

christianity_ezra_7_9.meaning: God protects those who follow him, making their journey safe and successful.
christianity_ezra_7_9.context: Ezra left Babylon in spring and reached Jerusalem five months later safely.

christianity_ezra_7_10.meaning: We should learn God's ways and teach others how to live right.
christianity_ezra_7_10.context: Ezra decided to study God's rules and share them with the people.

christianity_ezra_7_11.meaning: God can use leaders and laws to help his servants do important work.
christianity_ezra_7_11.context: The king gave Ezra a special letter with official permission to travel.

christianity_ezra_7_16.meaning: God wants us to give freely and joyfully to help build his house.
christianity_ezra_7_16.context: The king gave Ezra money and asked people to give more for the temple.

christianity_ezra_7_17.meaning: We should use our resources to honor God with proper and sincere worship.
christianity_ezra_7_17.context: Ezra was told to use the money to buy animals for special worship.

christianity_ezra_7_18.meaning: God trusts us to make wise choices that please him with what we have.
christianity_ezra_7_18.context: The king told Ezra he could decide how to spend the leftover money.

christianity_ezra_7_19.meaning: We must return what belongs to God and keep our promises to him.
christianity_ezra_7_19.context: Ezra had to bring the special holy items back to the temple in Jerusalem.

christianity_ezra_7_20.meaning: God often uses powerful leaders and resources to help his people finish important holy work.
christianity_ezra_7_20.context: The king tells Ezra he can use royal money to help rebuild the temple.

christianity_ezra_7_21.meaning: When God has a plan, he can make even strong rulers support and speed up the work.
christianity_ezra_7_21.context: The king orders all officials to help Ezra quickly with whatever he needs.

christianity_ezra_7_22.meaning: God provides enough for his work, and we should trust him to meet our real needs.
christianity_ezra_7_22.context: The king lists specific amounts of silver, food, and oil for the temple project.

christianity_ezra_7_23.meaning: Respecting God's ways keeps peace and safety for everyone, so we should always honor his rules.
christianity_ezra_7_23.context: The king says to follow God's commands to avoid angering heaven and harming the land.

christianity_ezra_7_24.meaning: God supports those who serve him, so we should not burden them with unfair financial demands.
christianity_ezra_7_24.context: The king gave Ezra a special order to protect religious workers from paying any taxes.

christianity_ezra_7_25.meaning: We need wise leaders who know God's rules to guide others and help them learn the truth.
christianity_ezra_7_25.context: The king told Ezra to pick wise leaders to teach and judge the people living far away.

christianity_ezra_7_26.meaning: We must take God's rules seriously because ignoring them brings real trouble and serious consequences.
christianity_ezra_7_26.context: The king said anyone breaking God's laws or royal rules would face serious punishment and consequences.

christianity_ezra_7_27.meaning: God can change even powerful leaders' hearts to help his people and support his holy work.
christianity_ezra_7_27.context: Ezra thanked God for making the king want to help rebuild the temple in Jerusalem.

christianity_ezra_8_8.meaning: Even small groups can be important in God's plan when they follow His guidance.
christianity_ezra_8_8.context: Zebadiah, son of Michael, led 80 men from Shephatiah's family.

christianity_ezra_8_9.meaning: Large numbers show God's support, but faith matters more than size.
christianity_ezra_8_9.context: Obadiah, son of Jehiel, brought 218 men from Joab's family.

christianity_ezra_8_10.meaning: Every person’s contribution helps build a stronger community for God's purposes.
christianity_ezra_8_10.context: The son of Josiphiah, from Shelomith's family, led 160 men.

christianity_ezra_8_11.meaning: Even a few faithful people can make a difference when they trust God.
christianity_ezra_8_11.context: Zechariah, son of Bebai, led 28 men from Bebai's family.

christianity_ezra_8_4.meaning: It shows the small group of faithful people who came back to rebuild their community.
christianity_ezra_8_4.context: A list of returning Jews from exile, led by Eliehoenai, with two hundred men.

christianity_ezra_8_5.meaning: It highlights the growing number of people committed to restoring their homeland.
christianity_ezra_8_5.context: Another group of exiles, led by Shecaniah, with three hundred men.

christianity_ezra_8_6.meaning: It reminds us that even small numbers can be important in God's plan.
christianity_ezra_8_6.context: A third group, led by Ebed, with fifty men.

christianity_ezra_8_7.meaning: It shows that many different families joined together to rebuild their nation.
christianity_ezra_8_7.context: A fourth group, led by Jeshaiah, with seventy men.

christianity_ezra_7_28.meaning: When God supports us, we can lead others and feel strong enough to face big challenges.
christianity_ezra_7_28.context: God helped me before the king and his advisors, and I gathered Israel leaders to go up.

christianity_ezra_8_1.meaning: Knowing where people come from reminds us of our shared history and the importance of community.
christianity_ezra_8_1.context: This lists the families of those who left Babylon with me during King Artaxerxes’ reign.

christianity_ezra_8_2.meaning: Recording family lines shows respect for ancestry and helps keep identity through generations.
christianity_ezra_8_2.context: Names of families: Phinehas’ son Gershom, Ithamar’s son Daniel, David’s son Hattush.

christianity_ezra_8_3.meaning: Listing many people highlights the strength of a united group and the value of each member.
christianity_ezra_8_3.context: Families of Shecaniah, Parosh, and Zechariah; a total of one hundred fifty men listed.

christianity_ezra_8_12.meaning: Us about unity and numbers in a community. Johanan and his hundred ten companions show the importance of having a strong group to face challenges together.
christianity_ezra_8_12.context: This verse is from the Bible's Book of Ezra (8:12) and talks about a group of people returning to Jerusalem from exile. It mentions Johanan, the son of Hakkatan, and a hundred ten males from the family of Azgad.

christianity_ezra_8_13.meaning: The importance of family and continuity. The names of the sons of Adonikam represent the continuation of their family line, emphasizing the value of family bonds.
christianity_ezra_8_13.context: This verse (Ezra 8:13) is also from the Book of Ezra. It talks about the sons of Adonikam and their names: Eliphelet, Jeuel, and Shemaiah, with sixty males.

christianity_ezra_8_14.meaning: The significance of unity and numbers. Uthai and Zabbud, along with seventy others, show the power of collective strength and unity.
christianity_ezra_8_14.context: Verse 14 (Ezra 8:14) mentions the sons of Bigvai, Uthai and Zabbud, and seventy males who joined the group.

christianity_ezra_8_15.meaning: Us about patience and unity. The group stayed together for three days, showing the importance of perseverance and waiting for others to join before moving forward.
christianity_ezra_8_15.context: Verse 15 (Ezra 8:15) describes how the group stayed at the river Ahava for three days, waiting for all the Levites to join them.

christianity_ezra_8_16.meaning: Ezra gathers a team of influential individuals to help with a religious task. Their roles include teaching and leadership. This shows the importance of teamwork and seeking guidance from knowledgeable people.
christianity_ezra_8_16.context: Ezra gathers a group of prominent men to assist in a religious mission. These men include Eliezer, Ariel, Shemaiah, Elnathan, Jarib, Elnathan, Nathan, Zechariah, Meshullam, Joiarib, and Elnathan. They are chosen as teachers and leaders for the task.

christianity_ezra_8_17.meaning: Ezra assigns responsible individuals to convey a message and request to Iddo and his helpers. This highlights the importance of clear communication and cooperation between leaders and their teams.
christianity_ezra_8_17.context: In Ezra 8:17, Ezra instructs these chosen men to go to Iddo, a leader at Casiphia, and inform him about the task. They are to inform Iddo and his temple servants to provide ministers for the house of God.

christianity_ezra_8_18.meaning: Ezra gathers dedicated families to support a religious task. Their involvement demonstrates the significance of unity, teamwork, and family support in achieving religious goals.
christianity_ezra_8_18.context: In Ezra 8:18, Ezra gathers Sherebiah and his family, along with Hashabiah and his family, to assist in the religious mission. These families consist of 18 and 20 members respectively.

christianity_ezra_8_19.meaning: Ezra turns to prayer for divine assistance in accomplishing a religious task. This shows the importance of seeking divine guidance and wisdom when undertaking sacred duties.
christianity_ezra_8_19.context: In Ezra 8:20, Ezra prays to God for guidance and success in the mission. He asks for understanding and wisdom to fulfill this sacred duty.

christianity_ezra_8_20.meaning: God values organized service and community support. We should help each other in our shared spiritual duties and tasks.
christianity_ezra_8_20.context: David and leaders gave many servants to help the Levites with their temple duties and work.

christianity_ezra_8_21.meaning: Humility and prayer prepare us for challenges. We should seek divine guidance and protection before starting difficult tasks or travels.
christianity_ezra_8_21.context: Ezra called for a fast by the river to humble themselves before God and seek protection for the journey.

christianity_ezra_8_22.meaning: Trust in divine protection over human force. Faith means believing God helps those who sincerely seek His will and guidance.
christianity_ezra_8_22.context: Ezra refused royal soldiers because he trusted God would protect those who seek Him with good intentions.

christianity_ezra_8_23.meaning: Sincere prayer and fasting can lead to divine help. God hears and answers the humble requests of His people.
christianity_ezra_8_23.context: The group fasted and prayed for safety, and God answered their request by granting them protection on the road.

christianity_ezra_8_28.meaning: We should give our best gifts to God, showing respect and gratitude for His blessings.
christianity_ezra_8_28.context: The people were preparing offerings of silver, gold, and vessels for God.

christianity_ezra_8_29.meaning: Honesty and careful handling of gifts are important when giving to God and to others.
christianity_ezra_8_29.context: They were told to keep the offerings safe until they were weighed before leaders.

christianity_ezra_8_30.meaning: Proper preparation and delivery of gifts help honor God and support His work.
christianity_ezra_8_30.context: The priests measured the offerings and brought them to Jerusalem.

christianity_ezra_8_31.meaning: Faith in God gives us safety and confidence when facing danger or uncertainty.
christianity_ezra_8_31.context: The group left the river, trusting God to protect them from enemies.

christianity_ezra_8_24.meaning: We should pick reliable people to handle important tasks because trust and responsibility are key to success.
christianity_ezra_8_24.context: Ezra chose twelve trusted leaders to safely carry valuable gifts back to Jerusalem for rebuilding the temple.

christianity_ezra_8_25.meaning: Being honest and careful with money shows respect for God and the community that supports good work.
christianity_ezra_8_25.context: They carefully counted the silver and gold that the king and people gave for the house of God.

christianity_ezra_8_26.meaning: God provides resources for his work when we are faithful and organized in our duties.
christianity_ezra_8_26.context: Ezra handed over huge amounts of silver and gold to the chosen leaders for the temple project.

christianity_ezra_8_27.meaning: We should treat sacred items with great care and honor because they represent our devotion to God.
christianity_ezra_8_27.context: The group also received special gold bowls and bright bronze vessels that were very valuable and precious.

christianity_ezra_8_32.meaning: Taking a short break helps you rest your body and mind before facing a big task.
christianity_ezra_8_32.context: The group arrived in Jerusalem and rested there for three full days before starting work.

christianity_ezra_8_33.meaning: It is wise to have honest people check important things to make sure everything is safe and correct.
christianity_ezra_8_33.context: On day four, trusted leaders carefully counted all the money and items brought back to the temple.

christianity_ezra_8_34.meaning: Keeping clear records of what you have helps you stay organized and prevents confusion later on.
christianity_ezra_8_34.context: They counted every single item by number and weight, then wrote down the total amounts.

christianity_ezra_8_35.meaning: Giving thanks to God with a happy heart shows you are grateful for being safe and home.
christianity_ezra_8_35.context: The people returned from exile and gave many animals as gifts to God in the temple.

christianity_ezra_8_36.meaning: Following the king’s instructions, the leaders supported the community and kept the temple strong.
christianity_ezra_8_36.context: Officials carried the king’s orders to local rulers, including those beyond the river, to help people and the temple.

christianity_ezra_9_1.meaning: The people were warned that mixing with others could lead to losing their own faith and values.
christianity_ezra_9_1.context: After the work finished, leaders approached Ezra, saying Israelites had mixed with foreign peoples and adopted their bad ways.

christianity_ezra_9_2.meaning: Leaders’ actions led to a loss of purity and a dangerous blending of cultures.
christianity_ezra_9_2.context: Ezra noted that leaders had taken foreign wives, causing Israel’s children to mix with other nations.

christianity_ezra_9_3.meaning: He showed deep grief and repentance for the nation’s wrongs and the loss of faith.
christianity_ezra_9_3.context: Hearing this, Ezra tore his clothes, cut his hair, and sat in deep sorrow.

christianity_ezra_9_4.meaning: True faith leads us to gather with others who care about doing right and avoiding sin.
christianity_ezra_9_4.context: Ezra gathered faithful people who feared God after seeing Israelites marry foreign wives and break holy laws.

christianity_ezra_9_5.meaning: We should show deep sorrow for our mistakes and pray honestly to God for help and forgiveness.
christianity_ezra_9_5.context: Ezra stood up from his shame, tore his clothes, knelt down, and prayed to God with open hands.

christianity_ezra_9_6.meaning: We must recognize how bad our sins are and feel true shame before a holy and good God.
christianity_ezra_9_6.context: Ezra felt too ashamed to look at God because the people had sinned greatly and their guilt was huge.

christianity_ezra_9_7.meaning: Sin brings serious trouble and pain to our lives, so we must stop sinning to avoid such suffering.
christianity_ezra_9_7.context: Ezra remembered that his ancestors had sinned for a long time, leading to war, slavery, and shame.

christianity_ezra_9_8.meaning: God gives small signs of hope and light to help us feel alive and keep going when life feels very heavy.
christianity_ezra_9_8.context: Ezra thanks God for saving a few people and letting them worship in the temple despite their hard slavery.

christianity_ezra_9_9.meaning: God does not leave us alone in hard times but helps us fix what is broken and build strong foundations.
christianity_ezra_9_9.context: Though they were servants, God helped them rebuild the temple and walls by winning favor with the Persian kings.

christianity_ezra_9_10.meaning: When we break God's rules, we should feel sorry and ask how we can make things right with Him.
christianity_ezra_9_10.context: Ezra feels deep shame because his people broke God's rules and ignored the clear commands given to them.

christianity_ezra_9_11.meaning: We must stay pure and avoid bad habits that pollute our lives and separate us from God's holy ways.
christianity_ezra_9_11.context: God warned through prophets that the land was dirty because of the bad actions of the people living there.

christianity_ezra_10_5.meaning: Making a public promise helps people stay honest and committed to doing what is right.
christianity_ezra_10_5.context: Ezra asked the leaders and people to promise they would follow the new rules.

christianity_ezra_10_6.meaning: Deep sadness shows how much we care about the truth and the well of others.
christianity_ezra_10_6.context: Ezra felt so sad about the people's wrong choices that he stopped eating and drinking.

christianity_ezra_10_7.meaning: Gathering together helps a community face hard issues and find a shared solution.
christianity_ezra_10_7.context: Leaders told everyone in the area to come back to Jerusalem to talk about the problem.

christianity_ezra_10_8.meaning: Clear rules and consequences help ensure everyone takes important matters seriously and acts fast.
christianity_ezra_10_8.context: They set a short deadline for people to arrive or lose their things and status.

christianity_ezra_9_12.meaning: Stay close to your true beliefs and do not mix with bad influences that weaken your spirit.
christianity_ezra_9_12.context: God told the returned Jews not to marry foreign women to keep their faith strong.

christianity_ezra_9_13.meaning: God is kind even when we fail, giving us a second chance to live and learn from mistakes.
christianity_ezra_9_13.context: Ezra admits the people sinned badly, but God showed mercy and let some survive the punishment.

christianity_ezra_9_14.meaning: Do not repeat old mistakes, because ignoring truth can lead to serious loss and total destruction.
christianity_ezra_9_14.context: Ezra worries that breaking God's rules again will make Him angry and destroy the remaining people.

christianity_ezra_9_15.meaning: We must be honest about our faults and trust in God's fairness, not our own good deeds.
christianity_ezra_9_15.context: Ezra stands before God, admitting they are guilty and cannot stand on their own merit.

christianity_ezra_10_1.meaning: When people truly feel sorry for their wrongs, they often gather together to show deep regret and unity.
christianity_ezra_10_1.context: Ezra cried and confessed sins while a huge crowd of people gathered around him to weep.

christianity_ezra_10_2.meaning: Even when we make big mistakes, there is always hope if we are willing to face them honestly.
christianity_ezra_10_2.context: A man named Shecaniah spoke up, admitting the group had broken rules by marrying outside their faith.

christianity_ezra_10_3.meaning: Making a clear plan to change our actions shows we are serious about doing what is right.
christianity_ezra_10_3.context: The man suggested making a formal promise to fix the problem and follow the old laws strictly.

christianity_ezra_10_4.meaning: Having support from others gives us the courage to make hard decisions and lead the way.
christianity_ezra_10_4.context: The crowd encouraged Ezra to take charge of the situation and not be afraid to act.

christianity_ezra_10_13.meaning: Serious problems need time and patience to fix. We must admit our faults and work hard to correct them.
christianity_ezra_10_13.context: Many people gathered in the rain, and Ezra said fixing this mistake takes more than a day.

christianity_ezra_10_14.meaning: We need fair leaders to help us follow the right path. Justice helps us find peace with God.
christianity_ezra_10_14.context: Ezra planned for leaders to gather in each city to judge those who broke the rules.

christianity_ezra_10_15.meaning: It takes courage to stand for what is right. We should support those who try to do good.
christianity_ezra_10_15.context: A few brave men stood up to stop the plan, and two others helped support their cause.

christianity_ezra_10_16.meaning: We must take our duties seriously and check our actions. Careful review helps us stay on the right track.
christianity_ezra_10_16.context: The returned people followed the plan, and leaders sat down to carefully check each name.

christianity_ezra_10_9.meaning: People felt deep shame and fear when they realized their actions had broken God's clear rules.
christianity_ezra_10_9.context: Many men came to Jerusalem quickly to sit before the temple and tremble in fear.

christianity_ezra_10_10.meaning: Leaders must speak the hard truth to help people see how their choices harm the whole community.
christianity_ezra_10_10.context: Ezra stood up and told the crowd that marrying outside their group made their sin much worse.

christianity_ezra_10_11.meaning: True change starts with honest confession and making a firm choice to follow God's guidance.
christianity_ezra_10_11.context: Ezra told the people to admit their faults and stop mixing with the local foreign families.

christianity_ezra_10_12.meaning: A community shows real commitment when everyone agrees to follow the right path together.
christianity_ezra_10_12.context: The whole group shouted back that they would do exactly what Ezra had told them to do.

christianity_ezra_10_17.meaning: Completing hard tasks quickly shows strong commitment to faith and obedience to God's clear commands for purity.
christianity_ezra_10_17.context: The people finished removing foreign wives from their homes by the start of the new year.

christianity_ezra_10_18.meaning: Even religious leaders must follow rules, showing that no one is above the law or exempt from correction.
christianity_ezra_10_18.context: Priests were found guilty of marrying foreign women, including leaders from the family of Jeshua and his brothers.

christianity_ezra_10_19.meaning: True repentance involves making a firm promise to change and offering a sacrifice to seek forgiveness.
christianity_ezra_10_19.context: They promised to divorce their wives and offered a ram as a sacrifice for their serious sin.

christianity_ezra_10_20.meaning: Sin affects many families, so everyone must examine their own life and correct wrong actions honestly.
christianity_ezra_10_20.context: Two men from the family of Immer, named Hanani and Zebadiah, were also found guilty of this sin.

christianity_ezra_10_25.meaning: This verse talks about the lineage of Parosh tribe members. It emphasizes family connections and genealogy.
christianity_ezra_10_25.context: This verse lists the names of descendants of Parosh, a tribe in the Old Testament. It mentions various sons and their relationships.

christianity_ezra_10_26.meaning: This verse describes the family members of Elam tribe. It highlights personal names and familial ties.
christianity_ezra_10_26.context: The verse lists the sons of Elam, another Old Testament tribe. It mentions their names and relationships.

christianity_ezra_10_27.meaning: This verse presents the offspring of the Zattu tribe. It focuses on names and familial ties within the tribe.
christianity_ezra_10_27.context: The verse lists the sons of Zattu, focusing on their names and connections within the tribe.

christianity_ezra_10_28.meaning: This verse discusses the family members of the Bebai tribe. It highlights personal names and familial connections within the tribe.
christianity_ezra_10_28.context: The verse mentions the sons of Bebai, detailing their names and relationships within the tribe.

christianity_ezra_10_29.meaning: These verses highlight the importance of family lineage and emphasize the repentance and restoration of the Israelite community after their exile. They show God's forgiveness and rebuilding of the community.
christianity_ezra_10_29.context: These verses list the names of descendants of Bani and their families in the Bible's book of Ezra. They are mentioned in the context of a group repenting and returning to Jerusalem after being exiled.

christianity_ezra_10_30.meaning: These verses highlight the unity and restoration of the Israelite community through repentance and returning to Jerusalem after exile. They emphasize the importance of family ties and God's mercy in rebuilding their lives.
christianity_ezra_10_30.context: These verses mention the sons of Pahathmoab and their families in the Bible's book of Ezra. They are included in a list of people repenting and returning to Jerusalem.

christianity_ezra_10_31.meaning: These verses showcase the diverse backgrounds of those returning to Jerusalem after exile, emphasizing their repentance and the unity of the Israelite community. They highlight God's forgiveness and the rebuilding of their lives.
christianity_ezra_10_31.context: These verses list the sons of Harim and their families in the Bible's book of Ezra. They are part of a group repenting and returning to Jerusalem.

christianity_ezra_10_32.meaning: These verses highlight the diverse backgrounds of those returning to Jerusalem after exile, emphasizing their repentance and the unity of the Israelite community. They showcase God's forgiveness and the rebuilding of their lives.
christianity_ezra_10_32.context: These verses mention the sons of Benjamin, Malluch, and Shemariah in the Bible's book of Ezra. They are part of a group repenting and returning to Jerusalem.

christianity_ezra_10_21.meaning: These names represent people from the Harim family during the biblical times. The verse teaches us about the importance of lineage and family connections.
christianity_ezra_10_21.context: In the book of Ezra, these verses list the names of descendants of Harim, a family in the biblical story. This verse focuses on five individuals: Maaseiah, Elijah, Shemaiah, Jehiel, and Uzziah.

christianity_ezra_10_22.meaning: These names represent people from the Pashhur family in the Bible. The verses emphasize the importance of family lineage and connections.
christianity_ezra_10_22.context: Verses v1 and v2 provide a list of sons of Pashhur, another family in the Bible. Verses mention six individuals: Elioenai, Maaseiah, Ishmael, Nethanel, Jozabad, and Elasah.

christianity_ezra_10_23.meaning: These names represent people from Levite and gatekeeper roles in the Bible. The verses highlight the diverse roles within a community and the importance of each person's contribution.
christianity_ezra_10_23.context: Verses v3 and v4 give a list of Levites and gatekeepers in the Bible. Verses mention seven individuals: Jozabad, Shimei, Kelita (also known as Eliezer), Pethahiah, Judah, and Eliashib.

christianity_ezra_10_24.meaning: These names represent people from Levite and gatekeeper roles in the Bible. The verses emphasize the significance of these roles in maintaining the community and its security.
christianity_ezra_10_24.context: Verses v3 and v4 provide a list of Levites and gatekeepers in the Bible. Verses mention six individuals: Shallum, Telem, and Uri.

christianity_ezra_10_41.meaning: The text records specific names to show that even leaders were guilty of this serious mistake.
christianity_ezra_10_41.context: This list names men from the tribe of Judah who broke the law by marrying outsiders.

christianity_ezra_10_42.meaning: The detailed list proves that this was a widespread problem among the returned Jewish people.
christianity_ezra_10_42.context: More names are listed here, continuing the record of men who married women from other nations.

christianity_ezra_10_43.meaning: It shows that the sin of mixing with other groups affected many different families and groups.
christianity_ezra_10_43.context: This verse lists the sons of Nebo who also married foreign women against God's clear commands.

christianity_ezra_10_44.meaning: This highlights the deep trouble they caused, as their children were born from these forbidden unions.
christianity_ezra_10_44.context: The writer explains that all these men had married foreign women and some had children with them.

christianity_ezra_10_37.meaning: True faith means making hard choices to stay close to God and his people.
christianity_ezra_10_37.context: These men are listed as leaders who agreed to leave their foreign wives.

christianity_ezra_10_38.meaning: Standing together in faith gives us strength to do what is right and true.
christianity_ezra_10_38.context: More leaders are named who joined the group deciding to follow God's rules.

christianity_ezra_10_39.meaning: Keeping promises to God shows that we truly care about doing what is right.
christianity_ezra_10_39.context: The list continues with more men who promised to obey the covenant.

christianity_ezra_10_40.meaning: Committing to God's ways helps us build a life that is pure and strong.
christianity_ezra_10_40.context: These final names complete the list of men who made a serious vow.

christianity_ezra_10_33.meaning: This list shows that everyone is responsible for their own choices, no matter who their family is.
christianity_ezra_10_33.context: Ezra lists the names of men from the family of Hashum who broke their faith.

christianity_ezra_10_34.meaning: Even small groups of people can make big mistakes, and their actions matter to the whole community.
christianity_ezra_10_34.context: The text names three specific men from the Bani family who made a serious mistake.

christianity_ezra_10_35.meaning: Staying true to your beliefs takes effort, and giving up can lead to serious problems later.
christianity_ezra_10_35.context: These are more names of men who chose to marry outside their own religious group.

christianity_ezra_10_36.meaning: We must always check our own hearts to make sure we are staying true to our promises.
christianity_ezra_10_36.context: The final names in this section are men who also chose to break their covenant.

christianity_nehemiah_1_1.meaning: Nehemiah, a Jewish leader, learns about the condition of his people in Jerusalem from his brother Hanani and other Judah travelers. This verse sets the initial situation.
christianity_nehemiah_1_1.context: This verse introduces Nehemiah, a Jewish leader, and mentions the month Chislev and his location in Susa, the palace.

christianity_nehemiah_1_2.meaning: Nehemiah learns about Jerusalem's hardships from Hanani and his companions. This verse highlights the challenges faced by the Jews after their captivity.
christianity_nehemiah_1_2.context: Hanani and other Judah travelers inform Nehemiah about the suffering and weakened condition of the remaining Jews in Jerusalem and the destroyed city and gates.

christianity_nehemiah_1_3.meaning: Nehemiah grieves upon learning about Jerusalem's ruins and the distress of the Jews. This verse emphasizes the sad state of Jerusalem.
christianity_nehemiah_1_3.context: Nehemiah hears about Jerusalem's destruction and the suffering of the Jews from Hanani and his friends.

christianity_nehemiah_1_4.meaning: Nehemiah reacts to the sad news about Jerusalem by showing sorrow, abstaining from food, and seeking God's guidance.
christianity_nehemiah_1_4.context: Upon hearing about Jerusalem's condition, Nehemiah mourns, fasts, and prays to God.

christianity_nehemiah_1_9.meaning: God's love and care for His people. It shows that even when they are far away, God will bring them back together if they return to Him and follow His commandments.
christianity_nehemiah_1_9.context: This verse is from the book of Nehemiah in the Christian Bible. Nehemiah, a Jewish man, prays to God about his people being scattered and asks for their return to their homeland. He mentions that even if they are far away in the farthest parts of the sky, God will bring them back.

christianity_nehemiah_1_10.meaning: God's sovereignty and His role as the Redeemer of His people. Nehemiah prays for God's blessings and protection for himself and his people.
christianity_nehemiah_1_10.context: In the same book of Nehemiah, Nehemiah prays to God about his people, acknowledging that they are His servants and have been redeemed by His great power and strength. He asks for God's favor and mercy.

christianity_nehemiah_1_11.meaning: This verse demonstrates Nehemiah's humility and devotion to God. He prays for divine assistance and asks for God's mercy before the king, showing that he remains cheerful even in the presence of authority figures.
christianity_nehemiah_1_11.context: Nehemiah prays to God, expressing his devotion and asking for divine help and favor in front of the king. He was not sad before the king.

christianity_nehemiah_2_1.meaning: Nehemiah's obedience and trust in God. He takes a significant step of faith by serving wine to the king, who is pleased and grants permission for the city's restoration.
christianity_nehemiah_2_1.context: This verse is from Nehemiah's account of his journey to rebuild Jerusalem. Nehemiah shares his experience of giving wine to the king, who was pleased and granted permission to rebuild the city walls.

christianity_nehemiah_1_5.meaning: Nehemiah appeals to God, acknowledging His qualities and asking Him to listen to the prayers of faithful people, showing humility and seeking mercy.
christianity_nehemiah_1_5.context: Nehemiah prays to God, asking for His mercy and asking to hear the prayers of the people who love and obey Him.

christianity_nehemiah_1_6.meaning: Nehemiah prays sincerely, recognizing his own sins and asking God to forgive the people of Israel, demonstrating humility and repentance.
christianity_nehemiah_1_6.context: Nehemiah prays, asking God to hear his words and show mercy to the people of Israel by acknowledging their sins.

christianity_nehemiah_1_7.meaning: Nehemiah admits Israel's wrongdoings, showing humility and remorse for their disobedience, and seeking God's forgiveness.
christianity_nehemiah_1_7.context: Nehemiah confesses the sins of the people of Israel, acknowledging their disobedience to God's commandments.

christianity_nehemiah_1_8.meaning: Nehemiah asks God to keep His promises and protect the people of Israel if they repent and obey His laws, showing faith and trust in God.
christianity_nehemiah_1_8.context: Nehemiah pleads with God to remember His commandments and not scatter the people among the nations if they trespass.

christianity_nehemiah_2_6.meaning: It is okay to ask for time to help others, and leaders should support good causes.
christianity_nehemiah_2_6.context: Nehemiah asks the king for time off to visit his hometown and check on its condition.

christianity_nehemiah_2_7.meaning: Having proper permission and support makes it easier to complete important and difficult tasks.
christianity_nehemiah_2_7.context: Nehemiah asks the king for official papers so local leaders will let him travel safely.

christianity_nehemiah_2_8.meaning: God often provides the specific resources you need when you ask with clear and honest purpose.
christianity_nehemiah_2_8.context: Nehemiah requests wood from the royal forest to build strong gates and walls for the city.

christianity_nehemiah_2_9.meaning: God often sends protection and help through other people when you are doing the right thing.
christianity_nehemiah_2_9.context: Nehemiah travels with the king's letters and a group of soldiers to protect him on the way.

christianity_nehemiah_2_2.meaning: Leaders often notice when people are hurting. It is good to be honest about your feelings.
christianity_nehemiah_2_2.context: The king noticed Nehemiah looked very sad and asked why he felt so down inside.

christianity_nehemiah_2_3.meaning: We feel deep pain when places we love are broken. This shows how much we care about home.
christianity_nehemiah_2_3.context: Nehemiah explained that his sadness came from seeing his hometown in ruins and destroyed by fire.

christianity_nehemiah_2_4.meaning: You can talk to God even in busy places. Prayer helps you find the right words to speak.
christianity_nehemiah_2_4.context: The king asked what Nehemiah wanted, and Nehemiah quietly prayed to God for help in that moment.

christianity_nehemiah_2_5.meaning: It is wise to ask for help respectfully. You should seek permission before starting big tasks.
christianity_nehemiah_2_5.context: Nehemiah politely asked the king for permission to go back and rebuild the old city walls.

christianity_nehemiah_2_10.meaning: People who want to keep power often feel threatened when others try to help the community grow and improve.
christianity_nehemiah_2_10.context: Two local leaders felt very angry and upset when they heard the king sent a helper to Israel.

christianity_nehemiah_2_11.meaning: Sometimes you need a short time to rest and observe the situation before you begin any major work.
christianity_nehemiah_2_11.context: Nehemiah arrived in the city and stayed there for three days before starting his big building project.
